The 𝑮​𝑾\bm{GW} compendium: A practical guide to theoretical photoemission spectroscopy

Dorothea Golze Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, Aalto University School of Science, 00076-Aalto, Finland    Marc Dvorak Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, Aalto University School of Science, 00076-Aalto, Finland    Patrick Rinke Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, Aalto University School of Science, 00076-Aalto, Finland
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The G​WGW approximation in electronic structure theory has become a widespread tool for predicting electronic excitations in chemical compounds and materials. In the realm of theoretical spectroscopy, the G​WGW method provides access to charged excitations as measured in direct or inverse photoemission spectroscopy. The number of G​WGW calculations in the past two decades has exploded with increased computing power and modern codes. The success of G​WGW can be attributed to many factors: favorable scaling with respect to system size, a formal interpretation for charged excitation energies, the importance of dynamical screening in real systems, and its practical combination with other theories. In this review, we provide an overview of these formal and practical considerations. We expand, in detail, on the choices presented to the scientist performing G​WGW calculations for the first time. We also give an introduction to the many-body theory behind G​WGW, a review of modern applications like molecules and surfaces, and a perspective on methods which go beyond conventional G​WGW calculations. This review addresses chemists, physicists and material scientists with an interest in theoretical spectroscopy. It is intended for newcomers to G​WGW calculations but can also serve as an alternative perspective for experts and an up-to-date source of computational techniques.

I Introduction

Electronic structure theory derives from the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics and describes the behavior of electrons – the glue that shapes all matter. To understand the properties of matter and the behavior of molecules, the quantum mechanical laws must be solved numerically because a pen and paper solution is not possible. In this context, Hedin’s G​WGW method [217] has become the de facto standard for electronic structure properties as measured by direct and inverse photoemission experiments, such as quasiparticle band structures and molecular excitations.

Electronic structure theory covers the quantum mechanical spectrum of computational materials science and quantum chemistry. The fundamental aim of computational science is to derive understanding entirely from the basic laws of physics, i.e. quantum mechanical first principles, and increasingly also to make predictions of new properties or new materials and new molecules for specific tasks. The exponential increase in available computer power and new methodological developments are two major factors in the growing impact of this field for practical applications to real systems. As a result of these advances, computational science is establishing itself as a viable complement to the purely experimental and theoretical sciences.

Hedin published the G​WGW method in 1965, in the same time period as the foundational density-functional theory (DFT) papers [231, 280]. While DFT has shaped the realm of first principles computational science like no other method today, G​WGW’s fame took a little longer to develop11 1 The theory directly comparable to DFT is the Luttinger-Ward formalism, not the G​WGW approximation. Here, we focus on the chronological development of practical electronic structure calculations with Kohn-Sham DFT or G​WGW.. DFT’s success has been facilitated by the computational efficiency of the local-density [280] or generalized gradient approximations [42, 312, 402] (LDA and GGA) of the exchange-correlation functional that make DFT applicable to polyatomic systems containing up to several thousand atoms. G​WGW, however, only saw its first applications to realistic materials 20 years after its inception [242, 184], due to its much higher computational expense. Soon after it was realized that G​WGW can overcome some of the most notorious deficiencies of common density functionals such as the self-interaction error, the absence of long-range polarization effects and the Kohn-Sham band-gap problem.

The G​WGW approach is now an integral part of electronic structure theory and readily available in major electronic structure codes. It is taught at summer schools along side DFT and other electronic structure methods. This review is intended as a tutorial that complements showcases of G​WGW’s achievements with a practical guide through the theory, its implementation and actual use. For G​WGW novices, the review offers a gentle introduction to the G​WGW concept and its application areas. Regular G​WGW users can consult this review as a handbook in their day-to-day use of the G​WGW method. For seasoned G​WGW users and G​WGW experts it might serve as a reference for key applications and some of the subtler points of the G​WGW framework.

In this review we take a more practical approach towards the G​WGW method. We will recap the basic theory starting from theoretical spectroscopic view point as a probe of the electronic structure. Aiming at G​WGW practitioners, we will illustrate how the G​WGW approach emerges from the theoretical spectroscopy framework as a practical scheme for electronic structure calculations. A more in-depth discussion of the theoretical foundations of many-body theory can be found in textbooks, e.g., [196, 145, 543, 355, 40], while the G​WGW theory itself is covered in excellent early reviews [220, 27, 218]. G​WGW began to flourish at the beginning of the 21st century and two reviews succinctly summarized the state of the field until then [31, 394]. Our review bridges the ensuing gap of almost twenty years, after which only several more specialized reviews addressed different aspects and applications of G​WGW calculations [446, 178, 407, 138, 72, 350, 176, 259] and complements a recent review [433].

A considerable part of our review is devoted to the presentation of different G​WGW implementations. We will discuss the practical considerations that G​WGW users have to make when they decide on a particular G​WGW implementation or code for their work. Moreover, we will guide the reader through computational decisions that might affect the accuracy of their G​WGW calculations and illustrate them with concrete examples from the G​WGW literature. An important aspect in this regard is the issue of self-consistency in G​WGW, which we cover in detail.

Although the G​WGW method might be best known for its success in predicting the band gaps of solids, we will present its diversity and discuss a range of different quantities that can be computed with the G​WGW method. Since no method is perfect, we will conclude with a critical outlook on the challenges faced by the G​WGW method and discuss ways to go beyond G​WGW.

We conclude this introduction with a quote from H. J. Monkhorst, who wrote in a laudation in 2005: It is therefore my conviction that, rather sooner then later, we will see a resurgence of the precise many-body approach to solid-state theory as we envisioned. Almost assuredly the G​WGW method will be the tool of choice. [370]. In 2019, we can say that Monkhorst was right.

II Theoretical spectroscopy

II.1 Direct and inverse photoemission spectroscopy

Spectroscopic measurements are an important component in the characterization of materials. Any spectroscopic technique perturbs the system under investigation and promotes it into an excited state. Experimentally, the challenge then lies in the correct interpretation of the system’s response. From a theoretical point of view, however, the challenge is to find (or develop) a suitable, accurate and, most of all, computationally tractable approach to describe the response of the system. Experimental and theoretical spectroscopy are often complementary and, when combined, they are a powerful approach.

Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) provides a rigorous and systematic quantum mechanical framework to describe the spectral properties of a system that connects central quantities like the Green’s function, the self-energy, and the dielectric function with each other. The poles of the single-particle Green’s function, the central object in MBPT, correspond to the electron addition and removal energies probed in direct and inverse photoemission, which is explained in detail at the end of Section II.1. In contrast, information about neutral excitations probed in optical or energy loss spectra can be extracted from the dielectric function. In this review, we will not address optical properties or other neutral excitations and instead focus on the single-particle Green’s function and its connection to direct and inverse photoemission spectroscopy.

In photo-electron spectroscopy (PES) [228, 409, 266], electrons are ejected from a sample upon irradiation with visible or ultraviolet light (UPS) or with X-rays (XPS), as sketched in Figure 1(a). The energy of the bound state ϵs\epsilon_{s} can be reconstructed from the photon energy h​νh\nu, the work function Φ\Phi and the kinetic energy EkinE_{\text{kin}} of the photoelectrons that reach the detector22 2 Throughout this article the energy zero is chosen to be the top of the valence bands for extended systems and the vacuum level for finite systems.

IPs=−ϵs=h​ν−Ekin−Φ,forϵs<EF.\text{IP}_{s}=-\epsilon_{s}=h\nu-E_{\rm kin}-\Phi,\quad\textrm{for}\quad\epsilon_{s}<E_{\rm F}. (1)

The ionization potential IPs\text{IP}_{s} is defined as the energy that is required to remove an electron from the bound initial state ss of the neutral sample, where the energy of the state is below the Fermi level (EFE_{\rm F}). It is always a positive number and related to ϵs\epsilon_{s} as shown in Equation (1).

By inverting the photoemission process, as schematically shown in Figure 1(b), the unoccupied states can be probed. This technique is commonly referred to as inverse photoemission spectroscopy (IPES) or bremsstrahlung isochromat spectroscopy (BIS) [117, 515, 160]. In IPES, an incident electron with energy EkinE_{\text{kin}} is scattered in the sample emitting bremsstrahlung. Eventually it will undergo a radiative transition into a lower-lying unoccupied state, emitting a photon that carries the transition energy h​νh\nu. The energy of the final, unoccupied state ϵs\epsilon_{s} can be deduced from the measured photon energy according to

−EAs=ϵs=Ekin−h​ν+Φ,forϵs≥EF-\text{EA}_{s}=\epsilon_{s}=E_{\rm kin}-h\nu+\Phi,\quad\textrm{for}\quad\epsilon_{s}\geq E_{\mathrm{F}} (2)

EA denotes the electron affinity, which we define as the energy needed to detach an electron from a negatively charged species and which is thus the negative of ϵs\epsilon_{s}. EA can be a positive or negative number. It is negative when the additional electron is in an unbound state, and positive when the electron is bound.

The experimental observable in photoemission spectroscopy is the photocurrent, which is the probability of emitting an electron with the kinetic energy EkinE_{\rm kin} within a certain time interval. It is related to the intrinsic spectral function A⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)A({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega) of the electronic system, given by the imaginary part of the single-particle Green’s function33 3 Atomic units 4​π​ϵ0=h=e=me=14\pi\epsilon_{0}=h=e=m_{e}=1, where ee and mem_{e} are the charge and mass of an electron, respectively, will be used in the remainder of this article.: [394, 14]

A⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=1π​Im​G​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)​sgn⁡(EF−ω),A({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)=\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Im}\>G({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)\sgn(E_{\rm F}-\omega), (3)

where ω\omega denotes an energy (frequency). The single-particle Green’s function, G⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)G({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega), is the probability amplitude that a particle created or destroyed at 𝐫{\bf r} is correlated with the adjoint process at 𝐫′{\bf r^{\prime}} −- it will be discussed in detail later. The actual dependence of the photocurrent on the spectral function is quite complicated because the coupling to the exciting light and electron loss processes in the sample, as well as surface effects, have to be taken into account. To our knowledge, no comprehensive theory yet exists for this relation and we therefore proceed with the discussion of the spectral function and will return to the photocurrent later.

The energies ϵs\epsilon_{s} in Equations (1) and (2) are the removal and addition energies of the photoelectron, respectively, and we refer to the transition amplitudes from the NN to the N±1N\pm 1-body states as ψs​(𝐫)\psi_{s}({\bf r}) (see also Section B.1):

ϵs=E⁡(N)−E⁡(N−1,s)ψs​(𝐫)=⟨N−1,s​|ψ^​(𝐫)|​N⟩}forϵs<EF\displaystyle\left.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\epsilon_{s}&=&E(N)-E(N-1,s)\\ \psi_{s}({\bf r})&=&\langle N-1,s|\hat{\psi}({\bf r})|N\rangle\end{array}\quad\right\}\textrm{for}\quad\epsilon_{s}<E_{\rm F}
ϵs=E⁡(N+1,s)−E⁡(N)ψs​(𝐫)=⟨N​|ψ^​(𝐫)|​N+1,s⟩}forϵs≥EF\displaystyle\left.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\epsilon_{s}&=&E(N+1,s)-E(N)\\ \psi_{s}({\bf r})&=&\langle N|\hat{\psi}({\bf r})|N+1,s\rangle\end{array}\quad\right\}\textrm{for}\quad\epsilon_{s}\geq E_{\rm F}

The states |N,s⟩\ket{N,s} are many-body eigenstates (wave functions in real space) of the NN-electron Schrödinger equation H^​|N,s⟩=E⁡(N,s)​|N,s⟩\hat{H}\ket{N,s}=E(N,s)\ket{N,s}, H^\hat{H} is the many-body Hamiltonian and E⁡(N,s)=⟨N,s​|H^|​N,s⟩E(N,s)=\langle N,s|\hat{H}|N,s\rangle is the corresponding total energy. The field operator ψ^​(𝐫)\hat{\psi}({\bf r}) annihilates an electron at point 𝐫\mathbf{r} from the many-body states |N⟩\ket{N} or |N+1⟩\ket{N+1}. The representation given in Equations (II.1) and (II.1) is particularly insightful because it allows a direct interpretation of ϵs\epsilon_{s} as the photoexcitation energy from the NN-particle ground state with total energy E⁡(N)E(N) into an excited state ss of the (NN-1)-particle system with total energy E⁡(N−1,s)E(N-1,s) upon removal of an electron in the photoemission process. Similarly, the addition energy that is released in the radiative transition in inverse photoemission is given by the total energy difference of the excited (NN+1)-particle system and the ground state.

To build a practical scheme for calculating the energies in Equations (II.1) and (II.1) we introduce the definition of the single-particle Green’s function44 4 We consider only the zero temperature GG and assume μ=EF\mu=E_{\mathrm{F}}.

G⁡(𝐫,σ,t,𝐫′,σ′​t′)=−i⁡⟨N|T^​{ψ^​(𝐫,σ,t)​ψ^†​(𝐫′,σ′,t′)}|N⟩G({\bf r},\sigma,t,{\bf r^{\prime}},\sigma^{\prime}t^{\prime})=-i\langle N|\hat{T}\{\hat{\psi}({\bf r},\sigma,t)\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\bf r^{\prime}},\sigma^{\prime},t^{\prime})\}|N\rangle (10)

where T^\hat{T} is the time ordering operator for the times tt and t′t^{\prime} and σ\sigma the spin. T^\hat{T} arranges the field operators so that the earlier time is to the right and acts on the ground state |N⟩\ket{N} first. GG allows for both time orderings: t>t′t>t^{\prime} or t′>tt^{\prime}>t. This definition of the Green’s function is particularly insightful because it illustrates the process of adding and removing electrons from the system, as done in photoemession spectroscopy. Assuming the time-ordering is as shown in Equation (10), ψ^†​(𝐫′,σ′,t′)\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\bf r^{\prime}},\sigma^{\prime},t^{\prime}) will create an electron with spin σ′\sigma^{\prime} at time t′t^{\prime} in point 𝐫′{\bf r^{\prime}}. This electron will then propagate through the system, until it is annihilated by ψ^​(𝐫,σ,t)\hat{\psi}({\bf r},\sigma,t) at a later time tt in position 𝐫{\bf r}. The Green’s function is therefore also often called a propagator. We will return to this propagator picture of GG in later sections of this review.

To make contact with Equations (II.1) and (II.1), we need to Fourier transform the Green’s function from the time to the energy axis. For a time-independent Hamiltonian this then produces the spectral or Lehman representation of GG [196, 145]

G⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=\displaystyle G({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)= limη→0+∑sψs(𝐫)ψs∗(𝐫′)×\displaystyle\lim_{\eta\rightarrow 0^{+}}\sum_{s}\psi_{s}({\bf r})\psi_{s}^{*}({\bf r^{\prime}})\times
×[Θ⁡(ϵs−EF)ω−(ϵs−i​η)+Θ⁡(EF−ϵs)ω−(ϵs+i​η)]\displaystyle\times\left[\frac{\Theta(\epsilon_{s}-E_{\rm F})}{\omega-(\epsilon_{s}-i\eta)}+\frac{\Theta(E_{\rm F}-\epsilon_{s})}{\omega-(\epsilon_{s}+i\eta)}\right] (11)

where we have assumed a spin paired system and summed over the spin quantum number shown in Equation (10). The two terms in brackets are for the two time orderings in GG. Θ\Theta is the Heaviside step function, which is zero for negative arguments and one for positive arguments55 5 For the remainder of the review, η\eta is always assumed to be a positive infinitesimal.. It kills any processes that do not obey the correct time ordering, as determined by the created/annihilated particle’s energy relative to EFE_{\rm F}. This representation illustrates that the many-body excitations of the system that are associated with the removal or addition of an electron are given by the poles of the single-particle Green’s function. The diagonal spectral function

A⁡(𝐫,𝐫,ω)\displaystyle A({\bf r},{\bf r},\omega) =1π​Im​G​(𝐫,𝐫,ω)​sgn⁡(EF−ω)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Im}\>G({\bf r},{\bf r},\omega)\sgn(E_{\rm F}-\omega) (12)
=∑sψs​(𝐫)​ψs∗​(𝐫)​δ​(ω−ϵs)\displaystyle=\sum_{s}\psi_{s}({\bf r})\psi_{s}^{*}({\bf r})\delta(\omega-\epsilon_{s}) (13)

then assumes the intuitive form of a (many-body) density of states.

II.2 The quasiparticle concept

In periodic solids, the crystal has special crystallographic directions so that spectra are direction dependent, with the direction indexed by a wave vector 𝐤\mathbf{k}. By varying the direction of the incident beam relative to the crystallographic axes (𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i}), one can map the 𝐤\mathbf{k} dependent PES spectra, as shown in Figure 2(a). This technique is called angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Figure 2(c) shows data from a typical ARPES measurement and Figure 2(b) a schematic of the spectral function at a single 𝐤{\bf k}-point. The spectra usually exhibit distinct peaks that are attributed to particle-like states but have a finite width. There can also be additional, broader peaks away from the main peak called satellites. However, the spectral function in Equation (13) contains only Dirac-delta functions which appear as infinitely sharp peaks. The broadening of the spectral function comes from the sum of many delta functions close in energy, which merge to form a peak of finite width. If the contributing delta functions are closely packed around one energy, the peak is attributed to a quasiparticle [304].

To further motivate the association of quasiparticles with particle-like excitations it is insightful to consider non-interacting electrons. In that case, the spectral function consists of a series of delta peaks

As​s′​(ω)=⟨ψs|A⁡(ω)|ψs′⟩=δs​s′​δ​(ω−ϵs),A_{ss^{\prime}}(\omega)=\langle\psi_{s}|A(\omega)|\psi_{s^{\prime}}\rangle=\delta_{ss^{\prime}}\delta(\omega-\epsilon_{s}), (14)

each of which corresponds to the excitation of a non-interacting particle, see Appendix A for the integral notation used in Equation (14). The many-body states |N⟩\ket{N} and |N±1⟩\ket{N\pm 1} become single Slater determinants so that the exact excited states are characterized by a single creation or annihilation operator acting on the ground state. The excitation energies ϵs\epsilon_{s} and the wave functions ψs​(𝐫)\psi_{s}({\bf r}) are thus the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the single-particle Hamiltonian.

When the electron-electron (or electron-ion) interaction is turned on, the exact eigenstates |N,s⟩\ket{N,s} are no longer single Slater determinants. As a consequence, the matrix elements of the spectral function As​s′​(ω)A_{ss^{\prime}}(\omega) will contain contributions from many non-vanishing transition amplitudes. If these contributions merge into a clearly identifiable peak that appears to be derived from a single delta-peak broadened by the electron-electron interaction, this structure can be interpreted as a single-particle like excitation – the quasiparticle. The broadening of the quasiparticle peak in the spectral function is associated with the lifetime τ\tau of the excitation due to electron-electron scattering, whereas the area underneath the peak is interpreted as the renormalisation ZZ of the quasiparticle. This renormalisation factor quantifies the reduction in spectral weight due to the electron-electron interaction compared to an independent electron, though the total spectral weight is conserved. We can combine these various arguments and say that the quasiparticle peak for state ss will exhibit the following shape:

As​s​(ω)≈1π​|Zsω−(ϵs+i​Γ)|.A_{ss}(\omega)\approx\frac{1}{\pi}\left|\frac{Z_{s}}{\omega-(\epsilon_{s}+i\Gamma)}\right|\quad. (15)

In contrast to the exact energies of the many-body states, which are poles of the Green’s function on the real axis, the quasiparticle poles reside in the complex plane and are no longer eigenvalues of the NN-body Hamiltonian. The real part of this complex energy is associated with the energy of the quasiparticle excitation and the imaginary part with its inverse lifetime Γ=2/τ\Gamma=2/\tau.

To develop a more intuitive understanding of quasiparticles, it is insightful to adopt a real-space picture. The quasiparticle concept can be explained by analogy with a crowd of people, as shown in Figure 3. Picture a group of people, such as at a concert or festival, all crowded into the same area. Not wanting to get too close to each other to preserve their own space, people in the crowd interact with each other. If one person gets too close to another, their mutual repulsion eventually takes over and separates them again. The exact description of the crowd requires the location of each individual person at all times. This is a very difficult task because of the constant interactions, or repulsions, between individual people. This collection of people and their occasional fluctuations are grouped together and labeled the ground state.

A new person arrives and pushes their way into the crowd. We can think of this new person as the electron in inverse photoemission that is injected into the system. The new person enters in a specific direction with a certain energy. As they enter the group, they repeatedly interact with other people as they continue their trajectory, as shown in Figure 3(c). These repeated interactions repel people in their immediate vicinity and form a small halo of free space around the incoming person. People seem to move out of their way on their journey, forming a polarisation cloud created by the absence of other people around them. The intruder’s motion and their polarisation cloud can be taken together to form a new composite object, a quasi-person, which appears as a slowed-down version of the newcomer. From far away, one does not need to describe the precise motion of all N+1N+1 people in the group, but only the motion of this quasi-person propagating through the crowd.

By analogy, a quasiparticle can then be considered a combination of an additional electron or hole in the system that interacts with its surrounding polarisation cloud. The situation corresponding to photemission spectroscopy is depicted in the bottom panel of Figure 3. As time increases, the bare hole left by removal of the interaction is screened. The quasiparticle therefore embodies an electron state with the perturbation of its own surrounding. The feedback via interactions of the particle with surrounding electrons is termed the self-energy. Over time, the propagating quasiparticle can decay into many different elementary excitations, giving it a finite lifetime. Essential quasiparticle properties are dispersion, lifetime, weight, and satellite spectrum. The latter arises from the collective excitations in the medium.

II.3 Comparison to experimental spectra

We have now identified quasiparticles as one possible source for peaks in experimental photoemission spectra. Before we introduce the G​WGW approximation as a tractable computational approach for calculating quasiparticle energies, we will first address the photocurrent, which is the quantity measured in direct photoemission experiments. Then we will briefly discuss the reconstruction of the band structure information, as well as other sources of peaks in spectrum.

Establishing rigorous links between the spectral function and the photocurrent is still a challenge for theory [218, 314, 367, 366]. The photocurrent J𝐤​(h​ν)J_{\mathbf{k}}(h\nu) is the probability per unit time of emitting a photoelectron with momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k} and energy Ekin,𝐤E_{\rm kin,\mathbf{k}} due to an incident photon with the energy h​νh\nu. The spectral function defined in Equation (3) describes the removal of an electron from the sample, but does not include intermediate steps on the way to the detector where the electron loses energy. Therefore, it does not correspond to J𝐤​(h​ν)J_{\mathbf{k}}(h\nu). However, the spectral function can be related to the photocurrent by using the sudden approximation [218, 219] assuming that the ejected photoelectron is immediately decoupled from the sample. J𝐤​(h​ν)J_{\mathbf{k}}(h\nu) is then given by [218]

J𝐤​(h​ν)=∑s,s′Δ𝐤​s​As​s′​(Ekin,𝐤−h​ν)​Δs′​𝐤,J_{\mathbf{k}}(h\nu)=\ \sum_{s,s^{\prime}}\Delta_{\mathbf{k}s}A_{ss^{\prime}}(E_{\rm kin,\mathbf{k}}-h\nu)\Delta_{s^{\prime}\mathbf{k}}\quad, (16)

where As​s′​(ω)=⟨ψs|A⁡(ω)|ψs′⟩A_{ss^{\prime}}(\omega)=\langle\psi_{s}|A(\omega)|\psi_{s^{\prime}}\rangle are matrix elements of the spectral function defined in Equation (3). Δ𝐤,s\Delta_{\mathbf{k},s} are matrix elements of the dipole operator which describe the coupling to photons. The dipole matrix elements capture the promotion of the electron to a highly excited state (often assumed to be a plane wave), i.e., they describe the transition between the initial and the final electron state. In this final state, the electron travels to the detector. On the way, it crosses the surface of the sample, which adds a further perturbation to its path and its energy. The transition matrix elements affect the amplitudes of the spectrum and add selection rules that give rise to the suppression or enhancement of certain peaks. In practice, one compares only matrix elements of the spectral function to the experiment disregarding the effects of the dipole matrix. Furthermore, it is often assumed that only the diagonal elements of the spectral function are dominating.

For the reconstruction of the band structure, e.g. with ARPES, the comparison between theory and experiment is hampered from the experimental side. In ARPES studies of crystalline materials, the emitted photons or electrons inevitably have to pass the surface of the crystal to reach the detector. Therefore, information about their transverse momentum k⊥k_{\bot} is lost. This is because the crystal’s translational symmetry is broken at the surface and only the in-plane momentum k∥k_{\parallel} is conserved. To reconstruct the three-dimensional band structure of the solid from experimental data, assumptions are often made about the dispersion of the final states [228, 409, 117, 515, 235]. Ab initio calculations as described in this article can aid in the assignment of the measured peaks. Either way, some layer of interpretation between theoretical and experimental band structures is required.

Apart from quasiparticle excitations, a typical photoemission experiment provides a rich variety of additional information. In core-electron emission for instance, inelastic losses or multi-electron excitations such as shake-ups and shake-offs lead to satellites in the spectrum. Satellites can also appear in the valence region. The outgoing photoelectron or the hole left behind can, for example, excite other quasiparticles like plasmons, phonons or magnons. This gives rise to additional peaks, the so-called plasmon or magnon satellites or phonon side bands, that are typically separated from the quasiparticle peak by multiples of the plasmon, magnon or phonon energy. The broad peak in Figure 4, which shows integrated spectra and therefore has no 𝐤\mathbf{k} dependence, near -40 eV is an example of a satellite. Satellites are collective effects that are not described within the quasiparticle picture.

III Hedin’s 𝑮​𝑾\bm{GW} equations

Having introduced the general Green’s function framework and quasiparticle concept, we are prepared to consider the concrete formalism for G​WGW. G​WGW is an approximation to an exact set of coupled integro-differential equations called Hedin’s equations [217], the full derivation of which can be found in Appendix B.

We build up Hedin’s equations from a perturbation theory perspective. We can conveniently represent the perturbation expansion for GG that we introduced in the time domain in Equation (10) and in the energy domain in Equation (11) with the Feynman diagram technique. Feynman diagrams are a pictorial way of representing many-body and Green’s function theory. We cover the necessary basics in this section and refer the interested reader to an excellent book on Feynman diagrams [361].

The perturbation expansion begins with the noninteracting Green’s function, denoted G0G_{0}. G0G_{0} is the probability amplitude for a noninteracting particle to propagate from one spacetime point to another. In the diagrammatic technique, G0G_{0} is represented by a solid line with an arrow. The ends of G0G_{0} indicate spacetime points. The generic notation 1=(𝐫1,t1,σ1)1=(\mathbf{r}_{1},t_{1},\sigma_{1}) refers to the spatial coordinate 𝐫1\mathbf{r}_{1}, time t1t_{1}, and spin variable σ1\sigma_{1}. G0G_{0}, shown in Figure 5, is one of the basic building blocks for the perturbation expansion.

GG is the probability amplitude for the interacting system that a particle creation at 2 is correlated with a particle annihilation at 1. The rules of quantum mechanics dictate that we must sum over all possible paths for the particle to move from 22 to 11 −- this generates the exact GG, which is represented by a bold, or double, line with an arrow in the diagram language. Every possible process between 11 and 22 contributes a different amplitude to the total GG. The different processes which connect 11 to 22 depend on interactions with other particles in the system at the times between t1t_{1} and t2t_{2}. Without these interactions, the problem is already solved with G0G_{0}.

Recall from the definition of GG in Equation (10) that GG contains two time orderings. The second time ordering implies that the annihilation process may come before the creation. Remember that the field operators in Equation (10) act on the interacting ground state. In the ground state, there is some charge for the annihilation operator ψ^​(𝐫)\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{r}) to “act” on, even without any preceding creation process, so that the reverse time ordering in GG makes sense. Feynman diagrams do not explicitly show both time orderings in GG, but it is important to remember that GG and G0G_{0} lines implicitly contain both time orderings.

The times between t1t_{1} and t2t_{2} are called internal times. We can add up all the processes contributing to GG in a certain order depending on the number of times the particle interacts with other particles in the system. These interactions occur only at internal times, and the number of internal interactions is the order of the diagram. To efficiently represent all these internal interactions, we use a dashed line to represent the interaction in the diagram. At a given order nn, we construct all possible processes, or diagrams, which connect nn interaction lines with G0G_{0} lines at 11 and 22. We connect all of the dashed lines appearing at internal times with additional G0G_{0} lines. There is a very specific set of rules for how these arrangements can be done. Wick’s theorem defines how to contract these pieces [145]. A simple principle is enough to demonstrate the idea, however. Because the Coulomb interaction is a two-body operator, each dashed line must have two G0G_{0} lines at each end. To compute the exact GG, the expansion must be taken to infinite order, n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, adding up all possible processes along the way. The process of building up all diagrams in the perturbation expansion is shown in Figure 6. A few example diagrams, as well as a couple of forbidden diagrams, are shown in Figure 7.

To go further with our analysis, we must dissect the internal structure of the diagrams and separate it into pieces. By considering the possible topologies of internal parts allowed by the contraction rules, we can group the parts into different categories. Here, the “topology” of the piece is determined by the number of G0G_{0} lines and interactions at two different times, without considering the internal structure between the two chosen times. Those parts which have two G0G_{0} lines sticking out are called a self-energy diagram. The full self-energy (Σ\Sigma) can be inserted between two G0G_{0} lines to form GG (one must also include the separate G0G_{0} term). Topologies which connect two G0G_{0} legs to an interaction line are labeled a vertex. Summing over all pieces with this topology creates the full vertex (Γ\Gamma), which depends on three spacetime points. Finally, the diagram parts which end in two dashed lines sum up to the effective, or screened, interaction (WW).

Conceptually, the vertex is the most difficult to understand. Figure 8 demonstrates the effect of the vertex in a specific example. The diagram shown in Figure 8(a) is meant to contain the exact vertex, Γ\Gamma. Γ\Gamma has three corners and can be inserted where two G0G_{0} lines meet an interaction line. By simply letting these three pieces meet without any internal structure, we replace Γ\Gamma with a single spacetime point, as shown in Figure 8(b). Alternatively, we could allow the vertex to include the curved interaction line shown in Figure 8(c). In that case, the vertex has internal structure.

Hedin’s equations can be interpreted as the self-consistent formulation of these topologically distinct building blocks. While Hedin followed a formal and systematic derivation, a heuristic motivation is to group all diagrams of a certain topology together and replace them with a single dressed, or renormalized, object with the same topology. A critical aspect of this replacement is their energy dependence. By replacing many diagrams of perturbation theory with a single object of the same shape, we reduce the number of objects to be computed. However, the information apparently missing due to the reduction in objects is encoded in the energy dependence of the dressed quantity. The final result, Hedin’s equations (Appendix B), are a compact and self-contained set of five integro-differential equations. Despite the reduction in the number of objects to be treated compared to the perturbation expansion, the functional differential equations coupling these pieces are extremely difficult to solve exactly.

Hedin recognized this difficulty and suggested the G​WGW approximation. As mentioned above, the vertex is the building block which has a single interaction connected to two G0G_{0} lines. Unlike the other building blocks, the vertex depends on three spacetime points instead of two, making it the most difficult to compute. To simplify the theory, Hedin suggested replacing Γ\Gamma with a single spacetime point. In Hedin’s equations, the exact self-energy is Σ=i​G​W​Γ\Sigma=iGW\Gamma. With the replacement Γ⁡(1,2,3)=δ⁡(1,2)​δ​(1,3)\Gamma(1,2,3)=\delta(1,2)\delta(1,3), Hedin’s approximation gives Σ=i​G​W\Sigma=iGW, hence the name of the G​WGW approximation. In this approximation, Hedin’s equations are

G⁡(1,2)\displaystyle G(1,2) =G0​(1,2)\displaystyle=G_{0}(1,2) (17)
+∫G0(1,3)Σ(3,4)G(4,2)d(3,4)\displaystyle+\int G_{0}(1,3)\Sigma(3,4)G(4,2)d(3,4)
Γ⁡(1,2,3)\displaystyle\Gamma(1,2,3) =δ⁡(1,2)​δ​(1,3)\displaystyle=\delta(1,2)\delta(1,3) (18)
χ0​(1,2)\displaystyle\chi_{0}(1,2) =−i​G​(1,2)​G​(2,1)\displaystyle=-iG(1,2)G(2,1) (19)
W⁡(1,2)\displaystyle W(1,2) =v⁡(1,2)+∫v⁡(1,3)​χ0​(3,4)​W​(4,2)​d​(3,4)\displaystyle=v(1,2)+\!\!\int\!\!v(1,3)\chi_{0}(3,4)W(4,2)d(3,4) (20)
Σ⁡(1,2)\displaystyle\Sigma(1,2) =i​G​(1,2)​W​(1+,2)\displaystyle=iG(1,2)W(1^{+},2)\, (21)

where the Hartree potential is included in the solution for G0G_{0}66 6 1+1^{+} means the time t1t_{1} evaluated at an infinitesimally later time. Such time infinitesimals appear in order to define the time-ordering for quantities meant to be evaluated in the instantaneous limit. The ground state density, for example, is time independent but must be written as n⁡(1)=−i​G​(1,1+)n(1)=-iG(1,1^{+}) so that the time-ordering makes sense..

These are the G​WGW equations, which are translated into the diagram language in Figure 9. There is one final important point regarding the reducibility of the quantities in Hedin’s equations. Σ\Sigma, χ0\chi_{0}, and Γ\Gamma in Hedin’s equations are all irreducible, which means that they cannot be broken into smaller pieces with the same topology. To generate the full, or reducible, quantity from its irreducible part, the irreducible component is iterated in a series similar to the perturbation expansion for GG. Series of this type are commonly called Dyson series, and Dyson’s equation refers to the equation for GG shown in Equation (17) (WW in Equation (20) also obeys a Dyson series). Dyson’s equation is of great importance in many-body physics, and we return to it in later sections in the context of self-consistent G​WGW. It is common in the literature to use the same symbol for both reducible and irreducible components with the same topology, especially when discussing the self-energy. Almost always, the symbol refers to the quantity as it appears in Hedin’s equations. When discussing or calculating the self-energy, this implies that one is interested in the irreducible self-energy.

In Hedin’s equations, the screened Coulomb interaction WW plays a central role. Screening is based on the simple idea that charges in the system rearrange themselves to minimize their interaction. In polarizable materials, screening is significant, and the effective interaction is noticeably weaker than the bare one. WW is also dependent on frequency or a time difference. The frequency dependence of WW is critical to both the physics and the numerical implementation of G​WGW. Even though the bare interaction is instantaneous, WW is time difference dependent because it is built from repeated bare interactions at different times. This series of bare interactions to form WW can be built by iterating the fourth line in Figure 9. The underlying G0G_{0} lines which connect the bare interactions in the WW expansion are themselves dependent on a time difference, so that if we vary the initial or final times the entire expansion changes magnitude. This series of repeated bare interactions connected by G0G_{0} is the microscopic mechanism for the quasiparticle screening concept developed in Section II.2. The frequency dependence of WW is what allows the system to relax and screen the quasiparticle. The G​WGW self-energy is similar to the bare exchange in Hartree-Fock theory, which can be written as the product of GG with vv. Given the similarity between the G​WGW self-energy and bare exchange, G​WGW can be thought of as a dynamically screened version of Hartree-Fock.

The G​WGW equations should still be solved self-consistently since all four quantities are coupled to each other. As with other nonlinear equations, including the equations of mean-field theories like Kohn-Sham DFT or Hartree-Fock theory, the G​WGW equations can be solved by iteration. In principle, the prescription is clear. Start from a given G0G_{0} and iterate Equations (17)-(21) to self-consistency (scG​WGW). However, remarkably few fully self-consistent solutions of the G​WGW equations have been performed in the last 50 years. The first calculations for the homogeneous electron gas (HEG) were reported at the turn of the previous century [234, 232, 169] and reported worse agreement with experiment on quasiparticle band widths and satellite structure compared to non-self-consistent calculations. They were quickly followed by calculations for real solids, like silicon and sodium [490, 293]. Self-consistency was then dropped for several years because of its high computational expense and the success of non-self-consistent approximations. More recent scG​WGW studies for atoms [113, 524, 525], molecules [471, 87, 351, 89, 86], conventional solids [297, 198] and actinides [296] have been reported. In practice, non-self-consistent calculations are much more common, and even self-consistent G​WGW calculations come in different types. scG​WGW is discussed in more detail in Section V.

IV The 𝑮𝟎​𝑾𝟎\bm{G_{0}W_{0}} approach: Concept and implementation

IV.1 The 𝑮𝟎​𝑾𝟎\bm{G_{0}W_{0}} equations

The lowest rung in the hierarchy of G​WGW approximations is the widely used G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} approach. Starting from a mean-field Green’s function, G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations correspond to the first iteration of Hedin’s equations. We denote the self-energy of such single-shot perturbation calculations Σ0\Sigma_{0}. Since we always refer to the single-shot self-energy in Section IV, we drop the label. Furthermore, we define the single-particle Hamiltonians

h^0\displaystyle\hat{h}^{0} =\displaystyle= −12​∇2+vext\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+v_{\mathrm{ext}} (22)

The spin channel is denoted by σ\sigma. Possible mean-field Hamiltonians are the Kohn-Sham (KS) or Hartree-Fock (HF) Hamiltonians.

From Dyson’s equation for GG, one can derive an effective single-particle eigenvalue problem referred to as the quasiparticle (QP) equation. The solutions of the QP equation are then given by

In the literature, G0G_{0} is often referred to as the “non-interacting” Green’s function. However, this is technically only correct if G0G_{0} is constructed from an initial calculation based on h^0\hat{h}^{0}. This is the definition of G0G_{0} in formal many-body theory. However, often times in the theoretical literature, the Hartree potential is included in the G0G_{0} solution and excluded from the self-energy. This is the case of starting the calculation from h^\hat{h} in Equation (23). For G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} in practice, we usually start from h^MF\hat{h}^{\mathrm{MF}}, which implies that we start from a mean-field Green’s function rather than a non-interacting one. Conceptually, such a mean-field G0G_{0} is closer to the interacting GG than the true G0G_{0}. This is precisely why the mean-field G0G_{0} serves as such a useful starting point for G​WGW calculations – it is closer to a self-consistent solution for GG than a true non-interacting G0G_{0} is. When consulting literature references, keep in mind that G​WGW calculations most likely refer to a mean-field G0G_{0}.

IV.2 Procedure

G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations are usually performed on top of KS-DFT or HF calculations. A flowchart for a typical G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation starting from a KS-DFT Hamiltonian is shown in Figure 10. Note that details of the flowchart depend on the treatment of the frequency dependence discussed in Section IV.3. Figure 10 starts with the KS energies {ϵsKS}\{\epsilon_{s}^{\rm KS}\}, KS orbitals {ϕsKS}\{\phi_{s}^{\rm KS}\} and the exchange-correlation potential vxcv^{\rm xc} from a DFT calculation. The exchange part of the self-energy Σsx\Sigma_{s}^{x} is directly computed from the DFT orbitals. For the correlation term Σsc\Sigma_{s}^{c}, the frequency integral over G0G_{0} and W0W_{0} must be computed, see Equation (33). If the integral is evaluated numerically, W0W_{0} is computed for a set of frequencies {ω}\{\omega\}. The procedure to obtain W0W_{0} is as follows: First, the irreducible polarizability χ0\chi_{0} (Equation (32)) is computed with the KS energies and orbitals. Second, χ0\chi_{0} is used to calculate the dielectric function ε\varepsilon (Equation (30)). From the inverse of ε\varepsilon and the bare Coulomb interaction vv, we finally obtain the correlation part of the screened Coulomb interaction, see Equations (29) and (34).

Since the QP energies appear on both sides of Equation (26), an iterative procedure is required. More precisely, the correlation term of the self-energy depends on ϵs\epsilon_{s} and must be updated at each step. Note that only G0G_{0} is a function of the QP energy, while W0cW_{0}^{c} depends solely on the frequencies of the integration grid. Therefore, W0cW_{0}^{c} can be pre-computed before entering the QP cycle, as displayed in Figure 10.

The correlation self-energy Σsc\Sigma_{s}^{c} is a complex quantity. However, the imaginary part of Σsc\Sigma_{s}^{c} is generally small for frequencies around the QP energy88 8 While the imaginary part might be small, it is nonetheless important as its inverse is proportional to the lifetime of the state., see Figures 11(a) and (b), where Σsc​(ω)\Sigma^{c}_{s}(\omega) is plotted for the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of the water molecule. To solve Equation (26), often only the real part of Σsc\Sigma_{s}^{c} is used, which simplifies the matrix algebra to real operations and reduces the computational cost.

A common technique to avoid the re-calculation of the self-energy at each iteration step of the QP cycle is the linearization of Equation (26) [178, 332, 586]. Assuming that the difference between QP and mean-field energies is relatively small, the matrix elements Σsc\Sigma_{s}^{c} can be Taylor expanded to first-order around ϵs0\epsilon_{s}^{0}:

ϵs\displaystyle\epsilon_{s} =ϵs0+Zs​⟨ϕs0|Σ⁡(ϵs0)−vMF|ϕs0⟩\displaystyle=\epsilon_{s}^{0}+Z_{s}\langle\phi_{s}^{0}|\Sigma(\epsilon_{s}^{0})-v^{\rm MF}|\phi_{s}^{0}\rangle (38)
Zs\displaystyle Z_{s} =[1−dd​ω​⟨ϕs0|Σ⁡(ω)|ϕs0⟩ω=ϵs0]−1.\displaystyle=\left[1-\frac{d}{d\omega}\langle\phi_{s}^{0}|\Sigma(\omega)|\phi_{s}^{0}\rangle_{\omega=\epsilon_{s}^{0}}\right]^{-1}\,. (39)

The self-energy matrix elements are now only required at the mean-field energies ϵs0\epsilon_{s}^{0}. ZsZ_{s} is known as the QP renormalization factor, because it measures how much spectral weight the QP peak carries (see also Equation (15) in Section II.2). The QP solution (main peak) is characterized by large ZsZ_{s} values, which lie around 0.7 to 0.8 for simple insulators, semiconductors and metals [31, 302] and around 0.9 for the molecules in Figure 12. Small ZsZ_{s} values indicate satellite features.

The linearization error depends on the state ss. The deviation from the full iterative solution usually is in the range of 0.1 eV for the HOMO, as shown in Figure 12 for a set of small molecules. The Taylor expansion of the QP equation becomes less and less accurate for larger binding energies because the absolute distance between DFT eigenvalues and QP energies increases (i.e. the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} correction increases). For the deeper valence states, the linearization error is already as large as 0.5 eV (see Figure 12).

Another alternative to iterating the QP equation is to find a graphical solution. As shown in Figure 11(a), the real part of the self-energy matrix elements is computed and plotted on a fine grid of real frequencies {ω}\{\omega\} around the expected solution. All intersections of the straight line ω+vsxc−Σsx−ϵs0\omega+v_{s}^{\rm{xc}}-\Sigma_{s}^{x}-\epsilon_{s}^{0} with Re⁡Σsc​(ω)\operatorname{Re}\Sigma^{c}_{s}(\omega) are then solutions of Equation (26). The intersection with the largest spectral weight ZsZ_{s} is the QP solution and is characterized by a small slope of Re⁡Σsc\operatorname{Re}\Sigma^{c}_{s}.

Another way to calculate the QP excitations is to compute the diagonal elements of the spectral function, As​s​(ω)A_{ss}(\omega), for a set of frequencies as shown in Figure 11(c). This is the most accurate procedure to obtain QP energies among the methods discussed here. As​s​(ω)A_{ss}(\omega) is computed from the complex self-energy (Σsc=Re⁡Σsc+i​Im⁡Σsc\Sigma^{c}_{s}=\operatorname{Re}\Sigma^{c}_{s}+i\operatorname{Im}\Sigma^{c}_{s}),

As​s​(ω)=\displaystyle A_{ss}(\omega)={} 1π​Im⁡Gs​s​(ω)​sgn⁡(EF−ω)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\pi}\operatorname{Im}G_{ss}(\omega)\sgn(E_{\rm F}-\omega) (40)
=\displaystyle={} 1π​Im⁡[(ω−ϵs0−(Σsc​(ω)+Σsx−vsxc))−1]\displaystyle\frac{1}{\pi}\operatorname{Im}\left[(\omega-\epsilon_{s}^{0}-(\Sigma^{c}_{s}(\omega)+\Sigma^{x}_{s}-v_{s}^{\rm xc}))^{-1}\right] (41)
×sgn⁡(EF−ω),\displaystyle\times\sgn(E_{\rm F}-\omega),

where we employed Equation (3), the Dyson equation, G=G0+G0​Σ​GG=G_{0}+G_{0}\Sigma G, and used only the diagonal matrix elements of Σ\Sigma. Figure 11(c) confirms that the solution at around ≈−12.0\approx-12.0 eV is the main solution. The spectral weight of the other solutions, e.g, the satellite peaks in the frequency range -30 to -25 eV, is indeed very small.

The aforementioned iterative procedure is computationally far more efficient than the graphical solution or the calculation of As​s​(ω)A_{ss}(\omega). The number of required QP cycles NQPN_{\rm QP} typically ranges between 5 to 15 and the self-energy only has to be computed for NQPN_{\rm QP} many frequencies. However, the spectral function takes also the imaginary part of the self-energy into account. This is essential for the accurate computation of satellite features in the G​WGW spectrum [433, 609]. Satellites fall usually in a region where Re⁡Σsc\operatorname{Re}\Sigma^{c}_{s} has poles, as demonstrated in Figure 11(a). In these regions, the imaginary part Im⁡Σsc\operatorname{Im}\Sigma^{c}_{s} exhibits complementary peaks and is non-zero (Kramers-Kronig relation), see Figure 11(b). Note that the graphical solution indicates the expected range of the satellite peaks, but does not predict their positions accurately because the imaginary part is omitted.

IV.3 Frequency treatment

The frequency integration in Equation (27) is one of the major difficulties in a G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation since both functions that are integrated, G0G_{0} and W0W_{0}, have poles infinitesimally above and below the real frequency axis. In principle, a numerical integration of Equation (27) is possible, but potentially unstable since the integrand needs to be evaluated in regions in which it is ill-behaved. However, a toolbox of approximate and exact alternatives is available. The most frequently used methods are summarized in the following.

IV.3.1 Plasmon-pole models

The simplest way to calculate the frequency integral is to approximate the frequency dependence of the dielectric function ε\varepsilon and thus the screened Coulomb interaction W0W_{0} by a plasmon pole model (PPM) [243]. The PPM approximation takes advantage of the fact that ε−1\varepsilon^{-1} is usually dominated by a pole at the plasma frequency ωp\omega_{p} [243]. This pole corresponds to a collective charge-neutral excitation (a plasmon) in the material. Assuming that only one plasmon branch is excited, the shape of ε\varepsilon can be modeled by a single-pole function

Re⁡ε−1​(ω)≈1+Ω2ω2−ω~2,\operatorname{Re}\varepsilon^{-1}(\omega)\approx 1+\frac{\Omega^{2}}{\omega^{2}-\tilde{\omega}^{2}}, (42)

where Ω\Omega and ω~\tilde{\omega} are two parameters in the model, whose squares are proportional to ωp2\omega_{p}^{2}, see Ref. [178]. ε\varepsilon, Ω\Omega and ω~\tilde{\omega} are matrices typically expressed in a plane wave basis because PPMs are mostly used for periodic systems. Note that Equation (42) holds for each matrix element and that we take the square of the matrix elements in Equation (42) and not the square of the matrix itself. Using a model function for ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}, the expression for W0W_{0} is greatly simplified resulting in an analytic expression for the self-energy, see Ref. [114].

The two parameters, Ω\Omega and ω~\tilde{\omega}, can be determined in several ways leading to different flavors of the PPM approximation [178]. The most common PPMs are the Hybertsen-Louie (HL) [243] and the Godby-Needs (GN) [183] model. The parameters in the HL model are obtained by requiring that the PPM reproduces the value of ε−1\varepsilon^{-1} in the static limit (ω=0\omega=0) and that the so-called ff-sum rule is fulfilled. The ff-sum rule is a generalized frequency sum rule relating the imaginary part of ε−1\varepsilon^{-1} to ωp\omega_{p} and the electron density in reciprocal space [258]. In the HL model, the low and high real frequency limits are exact and ε\varepsilon has to be calculated explicitly only at ω=0\omega=0. The parameters of the GN PPM are determined by calculating ε\varepsilon at ω=0\omega=0 and an imaginary frequency point i​ωp′i\omega_{p}^{\prime}, where ωp′\omega_{p}^{\prime} is typically chosen to be close to the plasma frequency ωp\omega_{p}. The latter corresponds to the energy of the plasmon peak in the electron energy loss spectra (EELS) and can be obtained from experiment. Alternatively, ωp′\omega_{p}^{\prime} follows from the average electronic density ρ0\rho_{0} per volume, wp′=4​π​ρ0w_{p}^{\prime}=\sqrt{4\pi\rho_{0}} [178].

A comparison between different PPMs, namely the HL, GN, Linden-Horsch [328], and Engel-Farid [131] model, can be found in Refs. [308, 527]. There it was shown that the GN model best reproduces the inverse dielectric function and the corresponding QP energies of reference calculations with an exact full-frequency treatment, such as the contour deformation discussed in Section IV.3.2. However, even the accuracy of the GN model decreases further away from the Fermi energy, i.e. for low-lying occupied and high-lying unoccupied states [302, 94].

While PPMs made the first G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations tractable [242, 243], full frequency calculations are now the norm, because the effects of the plasmon-pole approximation on the overall accuracy of the calculation are often hard to judge [527, 365]. Moreover, the imaginary part of the self-energy becomes non-zero only at the plasmon poles, which implies that QP lifetimes cannot properly be calculated with PPMs, see Equation (102) and Section VI.3. However, PPMs are still used in large scale G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations [114], for example for solids [247, 439], surfaces [335], 2D materials [126, 418, 120], graphene nano ribbons [544, 575] or polymers [230, 338].

The application of PPMs to molecules is conceptually less straightforward, because the dominant charge neutral excitations in molecules are not necessarily collective. This raises the question of how to define the plasma frequency ωp\omega_{p} of a molecule. Nevertheless, PPMs have also been used in benchmark studies for molecules, where mean absolute deviations of 0.5 eV from accurate frequency integration methods were reported [492].

The plasmon-pole model can be extended to an arbitrary number of poles, as proposed by Rehr and coworkers [517, 518, 262]. If many frequencies are required to determine the parameters in the model, the computational cost for the evaluation of Σ\Sigma is not necessarily reduced compared to full-frequency methods. However, multi-pole models are also well-defined for finite systems since the existence of a distinct plasmon peak is no longer an inherent assumption of the model [262].

IV.3.2 Contour deformation

The contour deformation (CD) approach is a widely used, full-frequency integration technique for the calculation of Σc​(ω)\Sigma^{c}(\omega) [187, 310, 192, 194, 189, 287, 57]. In the CD approach, the real-frequency integration is carried out by using the contour integral, see Figure 13. By extending the integrand to the complex plane, the numerically unstable integration along the real-frequency axis, where the poles of G0G_{0} and W0W_{0} are located, is avoided.

The integral along the contours shown in Figure 13 has four terms: an integral along the real (Re) and the imaginary axis (Im) and along the arcs.

i2​π∮d​ω′​G0​(ω+ω′)​W0​(ω′)=∫Re⋯+∫Im⋯+∫arc​Γ+⋯+∫arc​Γ−⋯\begin{split}\frac{i}{2\pi}&\oint d\omega^{\prime}G_{0}(\omega+\omega^{\prime})W_{0}(\omega^{\prime})\\ &=\int_{\rm Re}\cdots\penalty\ +\int_{\rm Im}\cdots\penalty\ +\int_{\rm arc\,\Gamma^{+}}\cdots\penalty\ +\int_{\rm arc\,\Gamma^{-}}\cdots\end{split} (43)

The contour integral is evaluated by taking the contours to infinity, which implies that the radius of the arcs is infinite. For infinitely large ω′\omega^{\prime}, G0​(ω+ω′)​W0​(ω′)G_{0}(\omega+\omega^{\prime})W_{0}(\omega^{\prime}) vanishes and the integral along the arcs of contours Γ+\Gamma^{+} and Γ−\Gamma^{-} is zero. Therefore, we can compute the real-frequency integral by subtracting the imaginary-frequency integral from the contour integral. After rearranging Equation (43) and using Equation (27), we obtain

Σ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=i2​π​∮d​ω′​G0​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω+ω′)​W0​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω′)−12​π​∫−∞∞d​ω′​G0​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω+i​ω′)​W0​(𝐫,𝐫′,i​ω′),\begin{split}\Sigma(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\omega)={}&\frac{i}{2\pi}\oint d\omega^{\prime}G_{0}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\omega+\omega^{\prime})W_{0}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})\\ -&\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega^{\prime}G_{0}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\omega+i\omega^{\prime})W_{0}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},i\omega^{\prime}),\end{split} (44)

where the second term is the integral along the imaginary axis.

The contours Γ+\Gamma^{+} and Γ−\Gamma^{-} are chosen such that only the poles of G0G_{0} fall into DΓ+D_{\Gamma^{+}} and DΓ−D_{\Gamma^{-}}, which denote the subsets of the complex plane encircled by Γ+\Gamma^{+} and Γ−\Gamma^{-}, respectively. The location of the poles of G0​(ω+ω′)G_{0}(\omega+\omega^{\prime}) depends on the frequency ω\omega at which the self-energy is computed. Recalling Equation (28), the poles of G0G_{0} lie at the complex frequencies

ωm′=ϵm0−ω+i​η​sgn​(EF−ϵm0).\omega_{m}^{\prime}=\epsilon_{m}^{0}-\omega+i\eta\penalty\ \mathrm{sgn}(E_{\rm F}-\epsilon_{m}^{0}). (45)

For ω<EF\omega<E_{\rm F}, these poles can enter only DΓ+D_{\Gamma^{+}} and must arise from occupied states. Our example in Figure 13 displays a case were ω<ϵ(HOMO−1)\omega<\epsilon_{\rm({HOMO}-1)}. Two poles, namely [ϵ(HOMO)−ω][\epsilon_{(\rm HOMO)}-\omega] and [ϵ(HOMO−1)−ω][\epsilon_{(\rm{HOMO}-1)}-\omega], fall into DΓ+D_{\Gamma^{+}}. For an even smaller ω\omega, more poles from deeper occupied states will shift into DΓ+D_{\Gamma^{+}}. Conversely, for ω>EF\omega>E_{\rm{F}}, the poles from the unoccupied states will enter DΓ−D_{\Gamma^{-}}.

We can now calculate the residues of the poles that are in DΓ+D_{\Gamma^{+}} or DΓ−D_{\Gamma^{-}}. Employing the residue theorem, the contour integral is then replaced by a sum over these residues:

i2​π∮d​ω′​G0​(ω+ω′)​W0​(ω′)=−∑ωm′∈DΓ+Res{G0(ω+ω′)W0(ω′),ωm′}+∑ωm′∈DΓ−Res{G0(ω+ω′)W0(ω′),ωm′}.\begin{split}\frac{i}{2\pi}&\oint d\omega^{\prime}G_{0}(\omega+\omega^{\prime})W_{0}(\omega^{\prime})\\ ={}&-\sum_{\omega_{m}^{{}^{\prime}}\in D_{\Gamma^{+}}}\text{Res}\left\{G_{0}(\omega+\omega^{\prime})W_{0}(\omega^{\prime}),\omega_{m}^{{}^{\prime}}\right\}\\ {}&+\sum_{\omega_{m}^{{}^{\prime}}\in D_{\Gamma^{-}}}\text{Res}\left\{G_{0}(\omega+\omega^{\prime})W_{0}(\omega^{\prime}),\omega_{m}^{{}^{\prime}}\right\}.\end{split} (46)

The integral along the imaginary frequency axis is smooth [442, 178] and the integration is performed numerically. The size of the frequency grid for the numerical integration needs to be carefully converged. For more details and a derivation of the final CD equations see, e.g., [189] or [194].

IV.3.3 Analytic Continuation

Analytic continuation (AC) from the imaginary to the real frequency axis is another method in our toolbox that enables an integration over the full-frequency range. The AC technique exploits the fact that the integral of the self-energy along the imaginary frequency axis,

Σc(𝐫,𝐫′,iω)=−12​π∫−∞∞dω′G0(𝐫,𝐫′,i​ω+i​ω′)×W0​(𝐫,𝐫′,i​ω′).\begin{split}\Sigma^{c}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},i\omega)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\omega^{\prime}G_{0}&(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},i\omega+i\omega^{\prime})\\ &\times W_{0}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},i\omega^{\prime}).\end{split} (47)

is smooth and easy to evaluate, unlike the integral along the real-frequency axis. However, the QP energies and spectral functions are measured for real frequencies. To return from the imaginary to the real frequency axis, the procedure is as follows: The self-energy is first calculated for a set of imaginary frequencies {i​ω}\{i\omega\} and then continued to the real-frequency axis by fitting the matrix elements Σsc​(i​ω)\Sigma^{c}_{s}(i\omega) to a multipole model. A common analytic form is, e.g., the so-called 2-pole-model [466, 442]

Σsc​(i​ω)≈∑j=12as,ji​ω+bs,j+as,0.\Sigma^{c}_{s}(i\omega)\approx\sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{a_{s,j}}{i\omega+b_{s,j}}+a_{s,0}. (48)

which has been widely used for G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations of materials [442, 155, 406] and molecules [264, 492, 586]. The unknown complex coefficient as,ja_{s,j} and bs,jb_{s,j} are determined by a nonlinear least-squares fit. From the identity theorem of complex analysis we know that the analytic form of a complex differentiable function on the real and imaginary axis are identical. Therefore, we can finally calculate the self-energy in the real-frequency domain by replacing i​ωi\omega with ω\omega in Equation (48).

An alternative multipole model function is the popular Padé approximant [332, 492, 587], which is more flexible but contains more parameters. In the Padé approximation, the complex fitting coefficients are not obtained by a nonlinear least-squares fit, but recursively from the matrix elements Σsc\Sigma^{c}_{s} and the imaginary frequencies {i​ω}\{i\omega\} [569].

In Figure 14 we compare the real self-energy matrix elements Re⁡Σsc\operatorname{Re}\Sigma^{c}_{s} obtained from the AC approach to an implementation on the real-frequency axis such as the CD method. The Padé approximation reproduces the self-energy exactly in the frequency range around the QP energy of the HOMO. The deviation in the HOMO-QP energy is smaller than 10-4 eV with respect to the CD results. By using a Padé approximant with a large number of parameters, even some features of the pole structure at higher and lower frequencies are reproduced, as shown in Figure 14. The 2-pole model, on the contrary, is significantly less accurate and yields an error of around 0.1 eV in the first ionization potential. For a comprehensive comparison between the Padé and 2-pole model see Ref. [492].

The reliability of the AC approach is limited to valence excitations, because the self-energy structure of deeper states shows poles closer to the QP solution. Our recent work [189] showed that the AC technique fails drastically to describe the complicated features of the self-energy for core states resulting in errors of 10-20 eV for the core-level binding energies. Furthermore, satellite features are difficult to obtain. As discussed in Section IV.2, satellites lie in regions, in which Re⁡Σsc\operatorname{Re}\Sigma^{c}_{s} has poles. As evident from Figure 14, these poles can only partly be reproduced by the AC.

The convergence parameters for the AC approach are the number of frequency points {i​ω}\{i\omega\}, for which the self-energy is computed, and the size of the frequency grid for the numerical integration over ω′\omega^{\prime}. In practice, the same grid is often employed for {i​ω}\{i\omega\} and {i​ω′}\{i\omega^{\prime}\} [264, 586].

IV.3.4 Fully Analytic Approach

The integral in Equation (27) can be carried out fully analytically. In this case, the Adler-Wiser sum-over-states representation of the polarizability introduced in Section IV.1 is not used. Instead we start from the reducible polarizability χ⁡(ω)\chi(\omega). In the spectral representation, χ⁡(ω)\chi(\omega) is given as sum of its poles nn in the complex plane

χ(𝐫,OPEN𝐫′,ω)=∑nρn​(𝐫)​ρn∗​(𝐫′)​(1ω+i​η−Ωn−1ω−i​η+Ωn).\begin{split}\chi({\bf r},&{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)=\\ &\sum_{n}\rho_{n}({\bf r})\rho_{n}^{*}({\bf r^{\prime}})\left(\frac{1}{\omega+i\eta-\Omega_{n}}-\frac{1}{\omega-i\eta+\Omega_{n}}\right).\end{split} (49)

The pole positions Ωn\Omega_{n} correspond to charge neutral excitation energies and ρn​(𝐫)\rho_{n}({\bf r}) denotes transition densities. Equation (49) would be exact for the exact Ωn\Omega_{n} and ρn​(𝐫)\rho_{n}({\bf r}). Both quantities are obtained by solving a conventional eigenvalue problem. The equations that are solved are identical to the Casida equations [93], except that for G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} the exchange-correlation kernel is omitted (otherwise it would be time-dependent density-functional theory).

The reducible polarizability χ⁡(ω)\chi(\omega) can then be expanded in terms of χ0\chi_{0} in a Dyson series

χ⁡(ω)=χ0​(ω)+χ0​(ω)​v​χ​(ω).\chi(\omega)=\chi_{0}(\omega)+\chi_{0}(\omega)v\chi(\omega). (50)

and we can thus rewrite W0W_{0} given in Equation (29) in terms of χ⁡(ω)\chi(\omega)

W0​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)+∫d​𝐫′′​d​𝐫′′′​v​(𝐫,𝐫′′)​χ​(𝐫′′,𝐫′′′,ω)​v​(𝐫′′′,𝐫′).\begin{split}W_{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)&=v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})+\\ &\int d\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime}d\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime\prime}v({\bf r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime})\chi(\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime},\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime\prime},\omega)v(\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime\prime},{\bf r^{\prime}}).\end{split} (51)

Inserting Equation (49) yields a pole expansion for W0W_{0}. The self-energy integral can then be solved analytically and we obtain a closed expression for Σsc​(ω)\Sigma^{c}_{s}(\omega):

Σsc​(ω)=∑m∑n⟨ϕs0​ϕm0|Pn|ϕm0​ϕs0⟩ω−ϵm0+(Ωn−i​η)​sgn⁡(EF−ϵm0),\Sigma_{s}^{c}(\omega)=\sum_{m}\sum_{n}\frac{\langle\phi_{s}^{0}\phi_{m}^{0}|P_{n}|\phi_{m}^{0}\phi_{s}^{0}\rangle}{\omega-\epsilon_{m}^{0}+(\Omega_{n}-i\eta)\sgn(E_{\mathrm{F}}-\epsilon_{m}^{0})}, (52)

where Pn​(𝐫,𝐫′)=ρn​(𝐫)​ρn∗​(𝐫′)P_{n}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})=\rho_{n}({\bf r})\rho_{n}^{*}({\bf r^{\prime}}). More precisely, Σsc​(ω)\Sigma^{c}_{s}(\omega) also becomes a sum over the poles Ωn\Omega_{n}. Equation (52) is therefore similar to the PPM approximation, except that we sum over the exact poles of W0W_{0} and not over the poles of a W0W_{0}-model function. A detailed description of the fully-analytic frequency treatment can be found in Ref. [495]. Equivalent expressions are also given in Hedin’s review article from 1999 [218] and were applied in Refs. [552, 70, 76].

IV.3.5 Comparison of accuracy and computational cost

In the previous sections three full-frequency integration techniques have been introduced: the CD, the AC and the fully-analytic approach. The CD and fully analytic method compute the self-energy directly for real frequencies. By design, the fully analytic approach is in principle the most exact one since it is parameter-free, except for the dependence on the basis set and the broadening parameter η\eta. However, the same accuracy can already be achieved with the CD using a moderately-sized numerical integration grid for the imaginary frequency term [189]. In the AC approach the self-energy is calculated on the imaginary frequency axis, which is fairly featureless. The accuracy of the AC approach depends on the features of the self-energy on the real axis and on the flexibility of the model function, which continues the self-energy to real frequencies.

Generally, QP energies of valence states are well reproduced [492], while the AC is likely to fail for deeper states as discussed in Section IV.3.3. In the PPM approximation, the self-energy integral is simplified by introducing a model function for W0W_{0}. The accuracy is therefore determined by the chosen model function and generally difficult to estimate.

The fully-analytic approach is the computationally most expensive method in our toolbox since solving the eigenvalue problem to obtain the poles of χ\chi is an 𝒪⁡(N6)\mathcal{O}(N^{6}) step, where NN defines the size of the system. The scaling of the CD and AC approach is generally lower, but depends on the details of the implementation. The CD method requires more computational resources than the AC methods due to the additional sum over the residues of the poles of G0G_{0}. The overhead is relatively small for QP energies of valence states, but increases for deeper states due to the steady increase of the number of residues. The PPM is computationally the most efficient method, because the dielectric function ε\varepsilon used to compute W0W_{0} has to be calculated only at a few frequency points to determine the parameters of the PPM.

IV.4 Basis sets

In any G​WGW implementation, the QP wave functions ψs\psi_{s} and also the mean-field orbitals {ϕs0}\{\phi^{0}_{s}\} are expanded in a set of normalized basis functions {φj}\{\varphi_{j}\}. Since in G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} the QP wave functions are approximated by the KS-DFT or HF ones, we expand in practice only ϕs0\phi^{0}_{s},

ϕs0​(𝐫)=∑jcs​j​φj​(𝐫),\phi^{0}_{s}({\bf r})=\sum_{j}c_{sj}\varphi_{j}({\bf r}), (53)

where cs​jc_{sj} are the expansion coefficients that have to be determined. Performing the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation in a basis transforms the expression for W0W_{0}, ε\varepsilon, and χ0\chi_{0} into matrix equations suitable for implementation in computer codes.

The basis set choice is often guided by the type of system under investigation. In the following we will introduce the most common basis sets with brief comments on their suitability.

IV.4.1 Plane waves

For periodic systems, the energy spacing between discrete enery levels can vanish, in which case the single-particle eigenvalues form bands. According to Bloch’s theorem [59], the single-particle states can be written as Bloch waves

ϕn​𝐤0​(𝐫)=ei​𝐤⋅𝐫⁡un​𝐤​(𝐫),\phi_{n\mathbf{k}}^{0}({\bf r})=\operatorname{e}^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot{\bf r}}u_{n\mathbf{k}}({\bf r}), (54)

where 𝐤\mathbf{k} is a wave vector in the first Brillouin zone and nn is the band index. The index ss that we had used in Equation (53) and throughout to label states now becomes the compound index n​𝐤n\mathbf{k}. The functions un​𝐤​(𝐫)u_{n\mathbf{k}}({\bf r}) have the periodicity of the lattice and can be expanded in plane waves {φ𝐆}\{\varphi_{\mathbf{G}}\},

un​𝐤​(𝐫)\displaystyle u_{n\mathbf{k}}({\bf r}) =∑𝐆cn​𝐤​(𝐆)​φ𝐆​(𝐫)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}c_{n\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{G})\varphi_{\mathbf{G}}({\bf r}) (55)
φ𝐆​(𝐫)\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathbf{G}}({\bf r}) =1Ω​ei​𝐆⋅𝐫\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\Omega}}\operatorname{e}^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot{\bf r}} (56)

where Ω\Omega is the volume of the periodic cell and 𝐆\mathbf{G} is a reciprocal lattice vector. Reciprocal lattice vectors 𝐆\mathbf{G} are given by 𝐆⋅𝐭=2​π​n\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{t}=2\pi n, where nn is a positive integer and 𝐭\mathbf{t} is a translation vector of the unit cell. G2G^{2} is directly proportional to the kinetic energy EE of a free electron. The size of the basis set is characterized by the largest 𝐆\mathbf{G} vector and is usually given in terms of the energy EE that corresponds to the largest reciprocal lattice vector, E=Gmax2/2E=G_{\mathrm{max}}^{2}/2. All 𝐆\mathbf{G} vectors with equal or smaller energies are included in the basis set.

The first G​WGW calculations [242, 243, 184] were performed for solids with plane wave basis sets. Also today plane waves are common in state-of-the-art G​WGW implementations, see Table 1 for a list of G​WGW codes. The real-space representation of G0G_{0}, W0W_{0}, ε\varepsilon, and χ0\chi_{0} given in Equations (28)-(32) can be easily transformed into a basis of plane waves by Fourier transforms. For expressions of these quantities in plane waves see, e.g., Ref. [241].

Plane wave basis sets are suitable for describing the slowly varying electron density in the valence region, where only the valence orbitals are non-zero. However, the valence wave functions tend to oscillate rapidly close to the nuclei due to orthogonality constraint with respect to the core orbitals. Representing these oscillations requires a large number of plane waves. Plane waves are therefore used in combination with pseudopotentials or the projector-augmented-wave methods [60] to approximate the effect of the core electrons. We will introduce the pseudopotential concept in Section IV.4.4 and return to plane waves in the context of the projector augmented wave scheme in Section IV.4.5.

IV.4.2 Localized basis sets

While plane waves are mostly used for periodic systems, they can in principle also be used for finite systems by placing, e.g., the molecule in a sufficiently large unit cell to avoid spurious interactions with the neighboring cells. However, large unit cells require a very large plane wave basis set and are therefore computationally expensive. Molecular systems can be more efficiently described by atom-centered localized basis sets.

The most common basis functions of this type are Gaussian basis sets

φα,l,m​(𝐫)=Nl​rl​Yl,m​(θ,ϕ)​e−α​r2,\varphi_{\alpha,l,m}(\mathbf{r})=N_{l}r^{l}Y_{l,m}(\theta,\phi)e^{-\alpha r^{2}}, (57)

where NlN_{l} is a normalization constant and Yl,m​(θ,ϕ)Y_{l,m}(\theta,\phi) are spherical harmonic functions given in spherical coordinates (rr, θ\theta, ϕ\phi). A Gaussian type orbital is characterized by the exponent α\alpha and the angular and magnetic quantum numbers ll and mm, which are dictated by the basis set selection. The design of Gaussian basis sets requires careful optimization regarding the number of functions, their respective angular momentum and exponents α\alpha. In quantum chemistry, Gaussian basis sets are widely used and ample experience exists in designing suitable basis sets for correlated methods such as coupled cluster theory. These Gaussian basis sets can then also be used in G​WGW calculations.

Another type of localized basis functions used in G​WGW calculations are numeric atom-centered orbitals (NAOs),

φl,m,μ​(𝐫)=Nl​uμ​(r)r​Yl,m​(θ,ϕ)\varphi_{l,m,\mu}({\bf r})=N_{l}\frac{u_{\mu}(r)}{r}Y_{l,m}(\theta,\phi) (58)

where uμ​(r)u_{\mu}(r) are radial functions that are not restricted to any particular shape. The radial part of NAOs is tabulated on dense grids and is fully flexible. Gaussian radial functions can be considered as special types of this general NAO form.

Slater type functions, which posses an exponential decay at long range and a cusp at the position of the nuclei, have been also used in G​WGW calculations [525]. However, this basis set type is less common.

Local basis functions, in particular NAOs that derive from atomic orbitals, are well suited to describe rapid oscillations of wave functions near the nucleus. They are therefore the obvious choice for QP calculations of core and semi-core states.

IV.4.3 Augmented basis sets

Augmented plane waves (APW) are another basis set type that includes the rapidly varying oscillations near the nuclei. APW methods use the so-called muffin tin approximation, which is a physically motivated approximation to the shape of the potential in solid state systems [356, 514]. The shape of the potential resembles a muffin tin: it is peaked at the nuclei and predominantly spherical close to it, while it is flat in between. Therefore, real space is partitioned into non-overlapping (muffin-tin) spheres ΩMT,a\Omega_{\text{MT},a} centered around each nuclei aa and interstitial regions ΩI\Omega_{\text{I}} between these spheres. The valence wave functions are then expanded in localized NAO-like functions (Equation (58)) inside the spheres and plane waves in the interstitial regions.

By construction, the APW basis sets produce wave functions with a discontinuity in the first derivative at the muffin-tin boundaries. The linear APW (LAPW) was proposed to guarantee that the solution in the muffin-tin matches continuously and differentiably onto the plane wave part in the interstitial region [17]. With this extension, the explicit form of the LAPW basis functions is

φ𝐆​(𝐫)\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathbf{G}}({\bf r})
={Ω−1​ei​𝐆⋅𝐫𝐫∈ΩI∑l​m(Al​ma​ula​(r)+Bl​ma​u˙la​(r))​Yl​m​(θ,ϕ)𝐫∈ΩMT,a\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\Omega^{-1}\operatorname{e}^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot{\bf r}}&{\bf r}\in\Omega_{\text{I}}\\ \sum_{lm}(A_{lm}^{a}u_{l}^{a}(r)+B_{lm}^{a}\dot{u}_{l}^{a}(r))Y_{lm}(\theta,\phi)&{\bf r}\in\Omega_{\text{MT,a}}\end{cases}

where ula​(r)u_{l}^{a}(r) and its derivative u˙la​(r)\dot{u}_{l}^{a}(r) are radial functions centered at the atom aa. The coefficients Al​mA_{lm} and Bl​mB_{lm} are determined such that continuity in value and derivative of the basis functions at the muffin-tin boundaries is ensured.

LAPW basis sets can be extended by additional local orbitals, LAPW+lo, that are completely localized in the muffin-tin spheres and go to zero at the boundaries. Inclusion of such local orbitals significantly improves the variational freedom, e.g., the description of dd and ff electrons [512]. It has furthermore been shown that these local orbitals are particularly important for the unoccupied state convergence in G​WGW calculations [156, 250, 249].

A general form of the LAPW method are full-potential LAPW (FLAPW) methods that make no approximations on the shape of the potential [592] and which are nowadays standard in LAPW codes. Recently a number of FLAPW G​WGW codes have emerged [157, 155, 154, 201, 252].

Linear muffin-tin orbital (LMTO) schemes are very similar to LAPW basis sets, except that the basis functions in the interstitial region are not plane waves [17], but for example smooth Hankel functions [364].

In these augmented basis sets it is straightforward to include core and semicore states in the Green’s function G0G_{0} (Equations (28)) and the polarizability χ0\chi_{0} (Equations (32)) and therefore in the self-energy. This, in principle, improves the description of QP excitations of valence states and band gaps, even though it has been found that the difference to carefully adjusted plane wave-based projector augmented-wave (PAW) calculations (see Section IV.4.5) is typically less than 100 meV [376]. However, the same study reported larger differences for deep-lying and very localized dd and ff states [376]. Core excitations are in principle also accessible with FLAPW basis sets. However, these have not been thoroughly investigated yet.

For local and semi-local DFT functionals, the (F)LAPW basis sets have become the ultimate accuracy reference, closely followed by NAOs [318, 317]. For G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, first steps in systematically benchmarking solids were made only recently [494]. For molecules, G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} benchmark calculations emerged during the last years and we will discuss them in Section IX.3. The jury is therefore still out on which basis set is most accurate for solids.

IV.4.4 Pseudopotentials

G​WGW calculations can be grouped in two categories: those that take all electrons of the system into consideration and those that partition into valence and core electrons. In this latter case, only the valence electrons enter the G​WGW (and the preceding DFT) calculation explicitly, whereas the effect of the core electrons is taken into account only indirectly, for example through a pseudopotential. Such core-valence partitioning is motivated by the observation that deep core states are relatively inert and do not contribute to chemical bonding. The advantage of using a partitioning scheme is that the electron number in the G​WGW calculation is reduced, which decreases the computational cost. An obvious disadvantage is that the core electrons may have an effect on the valence electrons, which will be difficult to include appropriately in the G​WGW calculation and then may lead to incorrect results.

Pseudopotentials have been the default way to partition electrons [356, 358].
