In a pseudopotential, the core electrons are removed and the Coulomb potential of the nucleus and the inner-shell electrons is replaced by a smooth effective potential that acts on the valence electrons. The potentials are generated from calculations of isolated atoms. They are constructed such that the wave function of the valence electrons match those of an all-electron calculation outside the core region or outside a chosen radius around the nuclei. Inside the core region, the functions are smooth and nodeless. Additional norm-conservation criteria [211, 33], which preserve the orthonormality condition for the pseudo wave function, are usually applied [561, 159, 188]. The resulting potential is finite at the origin of the atom and shallow. Pseudopotentials are mostly used in combination with plane waves since the smooth and shallow potentials greatly reduce the required plane wave cutoff and make plane wave G​WGW calculations with these basis sets feasible. In addition, pseudopotentials have been used for G​WGW calculations with localized functions to reduce the basis set size [57, 586].

The majority of pseudopotential development took place in DFT [358]. Optimizing the parameters in the pseudopotential to ensure transferability is a complex task and requires thorough testing [506, 188]. Transferability means that one and the same pseudopotential should be adequate for an atom in different chemical environments. Similar to localized basis sets, the parameters of pseudopotentials are precomputed, similar to localized basis sets, and then tabulated for download in libraries like the Pseudo-Dojo [493, 167].

In G​WGW, the consistency between pseudopotential and all-electron calculations will almost inevitably be violated. To be fully consistent, the DFT pseudopotentials would have to be cast aside and G​WGW pseudopotentials be used. However, no such G​WGW pseudopotentials have been developed until now, due to the complexity of the G​WGW self-energy, which does not lend itself easily to pseudoization. Even if we had G​WGW pseudopotentials, they would then have to first be used in the preceding DFT calculation, in which they would break the DFT core-valence consistency. Unless we perform fully self-consistent G​WGW calculations, we are stuck with an inconsistency dilemma.

Early efforts towards G​WGW pseudopotentials introduced core polarization effects into DFT pseudopotentials [504, 315]. By extending the G​WGW formalism to include core contributions in the dielectric screening and the self-energy, such core-polarization potentials have also been tried successfully in the G​WGW method [507]. However, developments in this direction did not continue. The default procedure today for plane wave G​WGW codes is to use only well tested DFT pseudopotentials for the required elements [195]. Care has to be taken that the scattering states (i.e. the unoccupied states) of the pseudopotential are described well and do not introduce ghost states [193]. If no good pseudopotentials are available, it is recommended to either generate customized pseudopotentials, use the PAW method or employ genuine all-electron basis sets. Pseudopotential approaches have to be employed with care in particular for materials with localized dd and ff electrons. Specific issues in G​WGW calculation of these materials are discussed in Section VI.

IV.4.5 Projector augmented-wave method (PAW)

The PAW method is commonly used in plane wave G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} implementations, see Table 1. It enables computational feasibility and ensures transferability between different chemical environments. The PAW method has been derived by Blöchl combining ideas from the pseudopotential method and LAPW basis sets [60]. The idea is to express the KS all-electron wave function ϕs0\phi_{s}^{0} for state ss in terms of a smooth auxiliary function ϕ~s0\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0} and correction terms, which restore the oscillating behavior in the core region. Note that for Bloch waves, the label ss contains the 𝐤\mathbf{k} and band index nn.

To construct ϕ~s0\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0}, we define a linear transformation 𝒯^\mathcal{\hat{T}} which establishes a connection between ϕs0\phi_{s}^{0} and ϕ~s0\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0},

|ϕs0⟩\displaystyle\ket{\phi_{s}^{0}} =𝒯^​|ϕ~s0⟩.\displaystyle=\mathcal{\hat{T}}\ket{\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0}}. (59)

Since the all-electron wave function is already smooth at a certain distance from the nuclei, we partition the space similarly to LAPW schemes: in atom-specific augmentation regions Ωa\Omega_{a} around the nuclei, where aa is the atom index, and an interstitial region ΩI\Omega_{\mathrm{I}}. The augmentation regions are characterized by the cutoff radii rcar_{c}^{a}, which should be chosen such that the augmentation spheres do not overlap. Outside the augmentation regions, ϕ~s0\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0} should be identical to the all-electron wave function. 𝒯^\mathcal{\hat{T}} should thus modify ϕs0\phi_{s}^{0} only in Ωa\Omega_{\mathrm{a}} and we define

𝒯^=1+∑a𝒯^a\mathcal{\hat{T}}=1+\sum_{a}\mathcal{\hat{T}}^{a} (60)

where the atom-centered transformation, 𝒯^a\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{a}, acts only within Ωa\Omega_{\mathrm{a}}.

The transformation operator is derived by introducing atom-centered functions as in LAPW, which is described in detail in Refs. [356, 470]. The all-electron wave function can then be rewritten as

ϕs0​(𝐫)=ϕs0~​(𝐫)+∑a(ϕsa​(𝐫)−ϕ~sa​(𝐫)),\phi^{0}_{s}(\mathbf{r})=\tilde{\phi^{0}_{s}}(\mathbf{r})+\sum_{a}(\phi^{a}_{s}(\mathbf{r})-\tilde{\phi}^{a}_{s}(\mathbf{r})), (61)

where the atom-centered hard and smooth auxiliary wave functions are denoted by ϕsa\phi^{a}_{s} and ϕ~sa\tilde{\phi}^{a}_{s}, respectively. “Hard” refers to rapidly varying functions in the core region. The concept of the PAW scheme is visualized in a simplified way in Figure 15. By adding ϕa\phi^{a} to ϕ~s0\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0} we obtain the oscillating behavior in the core region, but we have to subtract the smooth function ϕ~a\tilde{\phi}^{a} to cancel the contribution of ϕ~s0\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0} in Ωa\Omega_{a}. That implies that the following conditions must hold

ϕs0​(𝐫)=ϕ~s0​(𝐫)ϕsa​(𝐫)=ϕ~sa​(𝐫)}𝐫∈ΩIϕs0​(𝐫)=ϕsa​(𝐫)ϕ~s0​(𝐫)=ϕ~sa​(𝐫)}𝐫∈Ωa\left.\begin{aligned} \phi_{s}^{0}({\bf r})&=\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0}({\bf r})\\ \phi_{s}^{a}({\bf r})&=\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{a}({\bf r})\end{aligned}\right\}{\bf r}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{I}}\quad\left.\begin{aligned} \phi_{s}^{0}({\bf r})&=\phi_{s}^{a}({\bf r})\\ \tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0}({\bf r})&=\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{a}({\bf r})\end{aligned}\right\}{\bf r}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{a}}

The atom-centered auxiliary wave functions can be expanded in a finite set of local basis functions {φja}\{\varphi_{j}^{a}\} and {φ~ja}\{\tilde{\varphi}_{j}^{a}\} and a set of projector functions p~ja\tilde{p}_{j}^{a}, where ‘∼\sim’ indicates again smooth functions. These expansions are given by

ϕsa​(𝐫)\displaystyle\phi_{s}^{a}({\bf r}) =∑jφja​(𝐫)​⟨p~ja|ϕ~s0⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\varphi_{j}^{a}({\bf r})\Braket{\tilde{p}_{j}^{a}|\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0}} (62)
ϕ~sa​(𝐫)\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{a}({\bf r}) =∑jφ~ja​(𝐫)​⟨p~ja|ϕ~s0⟩.\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\tilde{\varphi}_{j}^{a}({\bf r})\Braket{\tilde{p}_{j}^{a}|\tilde{\phi}^{0}_{s}}. (63)

The variational object in a PAW calculation is ϕ~s0\tilde{\phi}_{s}^{0}. The latter is expanded using, e.g., a plane wave basis set, for which a low energy cutoff can be used due to its smoothness. The local basis sets and projector functions needed to compute the second and third terms in Equation (61) are tabulated for each element of the periodic table. For specific choices of these basis sets see, e.g., Refs. [291, 470]. Details regarding the practical implementation within a plane wave code are given in Ref. [291] and for real-space grid codes in Ref. [372, 132].

G​WGW calculations within the PAW schemes employ usually the frozen core approximation [508, 332]. The core states are localized at the atoms and confined in Ωa\Omega_{a}. In the frozen core approximation we assume that the KS core states are identical to the atomic core states α\alpha, i.e., ϕs0=φαa\phi_{s}^{0}=\varphi_{\alpha}^{a}. In this approximation, the decomposition given in Equation (61) is not used for the core states. However, the effect of the core on the valence states is correctly described.

The accuracy of the expansion in Equation (61) depends on the completeness of the set of localized basis and projector functions ({φja}\{\varphi_{j}^{a}\}, {φ~ja}\{\tilde{\varphi}_{j}^{a}\} and {p~ja}\{\tilde{p}_{j}^{a}\}). Achieving completeness is easy for occupied states, but practically impossible if ss corresponds to a high-energy empty state, which has been discussed by 273. However, for a G​WGW calculation, many of these high-energy empty states need to be included, which is explained in more detail in Section IV.5. These incompleteness issues lead to a violation of the norm-conservation for the unoccupied states, which can be the source of substantial errors, in particular for elements with dd and ff electrons. This error can be avoided using norm-conserving instead of the standard PAW potentials for G​WGW calculations [273].

IV.5 Basis set convergence

The first criteria for a reliable G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation is that the underlying DFT or HF calculation is converged. This convergence has to be checked for all basis set types. The second convergence criteria is the size of the basis set in the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation itself. In quantum chemistry it is well established that correlated electronic structure methods converge slowly with respect to the number of basis functions [265, 301, 275]. The same has been also observed for G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} [501, 156, 599, 70, 75, 495, 246, 492, 76, 586]. It has been demonstrated that the convergence rate of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} is comparable to other correlated methods such as second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation theory (MP2) and the coupled cluster singles, doubles and perturbative triples [CCSD(T)] method [75].

Converging G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} excitations within a plane wave basis set is straightforward since the cutoff energy can be continuously increased, see Figure 16(a). In addition, extrapolation schemes to the complete basis set limit have been reported to reduce the computational cost [273, 345, 195]. Conversely, for localized basis sets only a limited number of basis set sizes is available and a steady increase in size as for plane waves is not possible. Therefore, extrapolation techniques must always be used to obtain converged G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} energies. This is displayed in Figure 16(b), where the first IP of benzene is plotted with respect to the inverse of the basis set size. Shown are results for the Dunning basis set family cc-pVnnZ (nn=3-6) [122, 589], which was designed to smoothly reach the complete basis set limit. Increasing values of nn indicate increasingly large basis sets. The convergence is smooth, but very slow, as shown in Figure 16(b).

The extrapolation to an infinite number of basis functions is performed by a linear regression with respect to the inverse of the total number of basis functions. The extrapolated value of 9.17 eV in Figure 16 is 0.07 eV larger than the IP obtained at the cc-pV6Z level showing that even the largest basis set cannot converge the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} energies completely. This linear fitting procedure is a well-established scheme to extrapolate G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} energies and has been tested in large benchmark studies [492]. Alternatively, linear regression has also been performed with respect to Cn−3C_{n}^{-3}, where CnC_{n} is the cardinal number of the basis set, i.e., 3 for cc-pVTZ, 4 for cc-pVQZ , 5 for cc-pV5Z and 6 for cc-pV6Z. Extrapolation with respect to Cn−3C_{n}^{-3} is well-established for correlated methods [224]. The inverse of the basis set number corresponds roughly to Cn−3C_{n}^{-3}. The average difference between the two extrapolation schemes for G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} energies is indeed very small with 0.04 eV [492].

A common misconception in the plane wave community is that the number of unoccupied states that enter a G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation is a separate convergence parameter. The number of unoccupied states that can be resolved with a given basis set typically grows with the size of that basis set, i.e., the Hilbert space of that basis grows. This implies that more empty states enter the sums in the Green’s function (Equation (28)) and the polarizability (Equation (32)). Since it is computationally expensive to generate a large number of unoccupied states in the preceding plane wave DFT or HF calculation, plane wave G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} practitioners reduced the number of unoccupied states that enter the G​WGW calculation in order to save computational time [527, 494]. Localized basis sets on the other hand are significantly smaller and typically all virtual states are computed even in DFT-only calculations. Figure 16(a) gives an impression of the scale for the plane wave case. It displays the convergence of the band gap of wurtzite ZnO with respect to the number of bands (states) [599]. The convergence rate of ZnO is particularly slow [527, 156] compared to other semiconductors, e.g., silicon [157]. The band gap finally converges at around 30 Ha. At this point almost 3000 bands have been included in the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation.

While it might seem appealing to reduce the number of required unoccupied states to less than 3000, Figure 16(a) illustrates that a reduction is not possible due to the slow convergence. Since the number of resolvable, unoccupied states is coupled to the plane wave cutoff [494, 527, 166], one should always include the maximum number of bands in the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation for a given plane wave cutoff. Such a procedure also greatly simplifies the convergence study since only one and not two parameters need to be converged.

IV.6 Elimination of unoccupied state summation

The complications around the virtual state convergence raised in the previous section for plane wave basis sets can be bypassed completely by eliminating the explicit summation over unoccupied states in the Green’s function G0G_{0} (Equation (28)) and the polarizability χ0\chi_{0} (Equation (32)) [46, 181, 566, 590, 591, 435]. A practical method for building a perturbation theory without explicit reliance on unoccupied states was pioneered in the context of density functional perturbation theory (DFPT) [37, 190, 191]. Here we will briefly review how the DFPT concept can be transferred to G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}. For a general introduction to the DFPT formalism see 38.

The central object in DFPT is the response function that measures the response of a system to a perturbation Δ​V\Delta V. In the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} context, we are interested in the response to the introduction of an additional charge to the system at point 𝐫{\bf r}. The additional charge perturbs the charge density of the system. The response function mediates the charge density change and the perturbation. We now wish to calculate the response function without invoking the sum over states expression introduced in Equation (32).

We start with the change in the charge density Δ​n​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\Delta n({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega) given for a spin-unpolarized system by [181]

Δn(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=2∑ioccϕi0∗(𝐫′)×(Δ​ϕi0​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)+Δ​ϕi0​(𝐫,𝐫′,−ω)).\begin{split}\Delta n({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)=2\sum_{i}^{\rm occ}&\phi_{i}^{0*}({\bf r^{\prime}})\times\\ &(\Delta\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)+\Delta\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},-\omega)).\end{split} (64)

Here Δ​ϕi0​(𝐫,𝐫′,±ω)\Delta\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\pm\omega) is the frequency-dependent variation of the occupied mean-field state ii. Instead of expanding Δ​ϕi0​(𝐫,𝐫′,±ω)\Delta\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\pm\omega) in the basis of unperturbed mean-field states ϕi0​(𝐫)\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r}) it is calculated directly with the Sternheimer equation [37, 181]

(h^MF−ϵi0±ω)​Δ​ϕi0​(𝐫,𝐫′,±ω)=−(1−P^occ)​Δ​V​(𝐫,𝐫′)​ϕi0​(𝐫′).(\hat{h}^{\mathrm{MF}}-\epsilon_{i}^{0}\pm\omega)\Delta\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\pm\omega)=-(1-\hat{P}_{\rm occ})\Delta V({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r^{\prime}}). (65)

P^occ\hat{P}_{\rm{occ}} is a projection operator on the occupied states, P^occ=∑iocc|ϕi0⟩​⟨ϕi0|\hat{P}_{\rm{occ}}=\sum_{i}^{\rm occ}\ket{\phi_{i}^{0}}\bra{\phi_{i}^{0}}.

Sternheimer G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} formalisms differ in their choice of Δ​V\Delta V. There are two possible choices for Δ​V\Delta V. The first one is to set the perturbation to the bare Coulomb interaction v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}}) [435]

Δ​V​(𝐫,𝐫′)=v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′).\Delta V({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})=v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}}). (66)

This choice is known as non-self-consistent Sternheimer G​WGW. The Sternheimer G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} formalism is shown in Figure 17. Quantities that depend on 𝐫′{\bf r^{\prime}} are expanded in a basis {φk​(𝐫′)}\{\varphi_{k}({\bf r^{\prime}})\}, see Equation(53), and both sides of Equation (65) are projected onto φl​(𝐫′)\varphi_{l}({\bf r^{\prime}}). This leads to a linear set of equations with a parametric dependence on 𝐫{\bf r} and ±ω\pm\omega. Solving the Sternheimer equation for each real-space grid point 𝐫{\bf r} and the frequencies ±ω\pm\omega yields Δ​ϕi0​(𝐫,𝐫′,±ωCLOSE\Delta\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\pm\omega) for the occupied state ii. From the latter we can evaluate the induced charge density Δ​n\Delta n. The dielectric function given in Equation (30) can be rewritten in terms of Δ​n\Delta n [435, 303]

ε⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=δ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)−Δ​n​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω).\varepsilon({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)=\delta({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})-\Delta n({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega). (67)

W0W_{0} is then calculated from the inverse of ε\varepsilon according to Equation (29) as usual.

The second choice for Δ​V\Delta V is to set it to the screened Coulomb interaction

Δ​V​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=W0​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω),\Delta V({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega)=W_{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega), (68)

leading to the self-consistent Sternheimer G​WGW formalism introduced by 181. In this scheme, the (self-consistent) induced charge density Δ​nSC\Delta n^{\rm{SC}} generates a potential Δ​Vscr\Delta V_{\rm{scr}}, which screens the bare Coulomb potential vv due to the perturbative charge in the system. From Δ​Vscr\Delta V_{\rm{scr}} we can directly calculate W0W_{0} as

Δ​Vscr​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\displaystyle\Delta V_{\rm{scr}}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega) =∫d​𝐫′′​Δ​nSC​(𝐫,𝐫′′,ω)​v​(𝐫′′​𝐫′)\displaystyle=\int d\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime}\Delta n^{\rm{SC}}({\bf r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime},\omega)v(\mathbf{r}^{\prime\prime}{\bf r^{\prime}}) (69)
W0​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\displaystyle W_{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega) =v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)+Δ​Vscr​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω).\displaystyle=v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})+\Delta V_{\rm{scr}}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega). (70)

It can be shown that Equation (70) is equivalent to Equation (29) [181]. Since W0W_{0} appears on the right-hand side of Equation (65), it must be solved self-consistently. In the first step, W0W_{0} is initialized with vv. From the solutions of the Sternheimer equation, we calculate Δ​nSC\Delta n^{\rm{SC}}, Δ​Vscr\Delta V_{\rm{scr}} and finally W0W_{0}.

Both schemes yield W0W_{0}, but the non-self-consistent approach requires fewer steps. However, the dimensions of the dielectric matrix increase with system size and its inversion might become a bottleneck for large systems, in particular when using plane wave basis sets. In this case the self-consistent scheme might be more efficient.

The two schemes discussed so far address the elimination of empty states in W0W_{0}. Removing the sum over virtual states in G0G_{0} is also possible by using a similar strategy as for W0W_{0}, see 181 for a detailed description. Once G0G_{0} and W0W_{0} have been obtained, the self-energy is composed as usual and the frequency integration is performed with the methods described in Section IV.3. Sternheimer approaches have been implemented for plasmon pole models [435], the analytic continuation [181] and contour deformation [194].

The Sternheimer G​WGW approach is primarily used in plane wave implementations [303, 435, 194, 382, 406]. We are only aware of one non-plane wave implementation using mixed representations of real space and localized basis sets [238, 239]. As discussed in Section IV.5, converging a G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation with plane waves requires a very large number of empty states. The calculation of all empty states in the preceding DFT or HF calculation is computationally expensive and can easily become a computational and storage bottleneck. In the Sternheimer approach, the preceding DFT step is significantly simplified since only occupied states have to be calculated. For localized basis sets, no such benefit is found in DFPT or Sternheimer since the number of virtual states is typically not that large and rarely a bottleneck [497].

Sternheimer G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} saves not only computational time in the preceding mean-field calculation, but also by not having to carry out the sums over states in G0G_{0} and χ0\chi_{0}. However, it concomitantly loses time in the Sternheimer iterations. To our knowledge, a detailed comparison of the computational cost to conventional G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} implementations has not been reported yet. To speed up Sternheimer G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, projection techniques for representing the dielectric matrix in an optimal, smaller basis [382, 406, 194, 590, 591] and Lanczos-chain algorithms that efficiently obtain the Sternheimer solution over a broad frequency range [566] have been developed. Furthermore, all the Sternheimer equations, that need to be solved for each 𝐫{\bf r} and ω\omega, are independent from each other facilitating massively parallel implementation [194, 486].

The Sternheimer approach does not reduce the basis set size, i.e., the plane wave cutoff or equivalently the size of the real-space grid, nor does it change the formal scaling of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} with respect to system size. However, it is an elegant way to facilitate easier convergence, since the temptation of converging the number of virtual states separately is removed.

A modified Sternheimer ansatz has been developed for FLAPW basis sets which accounts for response contributions outside the Hilbert space spanned by the basis set [51, 50, 52]. This modified approach thus allows the basis set size to be decreased, unlike the classical Sternheimer technique. The explicit summation over unoccupied states is not completely removed, but the number of empty states needed for convergence is strongly reduced.

IV.7 Starting point dependence and optimization

The results of a G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation depend on the wave functions {ϕs0}\{\phi_{s}^{0}\} and the energies ϵs0\epsilon_{s}^{0} that are used as input for the Green’s function (G0G_{0}) and the screened Coulomb interaction (W0W_{0}). The single-particle wave functions and energies are determined by the choice of the single-particle mean-field Hamiltonian h^MF\hat{h}^{\mathrm{MF}}, e.g., by the chosen DFT functional. To denote this dependence, we will introduce the notation G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@s​t​a​r​t​i​n​g​p​o​i​n​tstarting\>point.

IV.7.1 How severe is the dependence on the reference state?

Until the early 2000s, the majority of all G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations were based on DFT calculations using the local-density approximation (LDA) or a generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [31, 27, 394]. With the advent of exact-exchange based DFT functionals in the solid state community and the proliferation of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} codes that are based on quantum chemical codes, a more diverse range of starting points became available. It was soon realized that G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} can exhibit a pronounced starting-point dependence for semiconductors [445, 158]. In the last years, the starting point dependence has also been intensively discussed for molecules [284, 351, 75, 163, 164, 82].

Figure 18 illustrates the starting-point dependence for the HOMO of the water molecule. For the underlying DFT calculations, the PBE-based hybrid (PBEh) functional family [403, 134, 1] was scanned. The PBEh functional family is characterized by an adjustable fraction α\alpha of HF exchange. The exchange-correlation energy ExcE_{\mathrm{xc}} is therefore α\alpha-dependent and given by

Exc=α​ExEX+(1−α)​ExPBE+EcPBE,α∈[0,1],E_{\mathrm{xc}}=\alpha E_{x}^{\mathrm{EX}}+(1-\alpha)E_{x}^{\mathrm{PBE}}+E_{c}^{\mathrm{PBE}},\quad\alpha\in[0,1], (71)

where ExEXE_{x}^{\mathrm{EX}} denotes the HF exchange energy. ExPBEE_{x}^{\mathrm{PBE}} and EcPBEE_{c}^{\mathrm{PBE}} are the PBE exchange and correlation energy, respectively. To illustrate the starting point dependence in G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, the mixing parameter α\alpha in PBEh was varied from 0 to 1 and then a subsequent G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation was performed. The resulting G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} HOMO energies shown in Figure 18 span a range of more than 1 eV. Although a 1 eV spread appears large, it is much smaller than the range of the corresponding mean-field energies ϵHOMO0\epsilon^{0}_{\rm{HOMO}} that decrease from -7 eV to -14 eV with increasing α\alpha.

The strong dependence of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} on the starting point can be largely attributed to over- and under-screening. From the Adler-Wiser expression for χ0\chi_{0} (Equation (32)) it can be deduced that the screening strength in G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} is inversely proportional to the eigenvalue gap of the starting point. Since HF typically overestimates gaps, it will under-screen. PBE, on the other hand, underestimates gaps and therefore over-screens.

Another source of error in the KS orbital energies is the spurious self-interaction term [405]. The one-electron self-interaction error (SIE) arises from an incomplete cancellation of the unphysical electrostatic Hartree energy of an electron with itself by the exchange-correlation term. The SIE is more pronounced for localized than delocalized orbitals [283]. This can be intuitively understood: an electron in a localized orbital has a stronger self-interaction because its wave function is more confined. As a result, the localized orbitals are destabilized with respect to more delocalized orbitals. This can lead to a wrong ordering of the orbital energies in the underlying DFT calculations, which carries over to the G​WGW spectrum. The SIE can be mitigated by a larger amount of exact exchange, which also restores the correct ordering for the QP energies [352, 351, 284].

The G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} starting point dependence generally lies in the range of 1.0 eV for HOMO energies of molecules [351], but increases for deeper states. For solids, the spread can exceed 2 eV for the band gap [158]. This beckons for a judicious choice of the starting point in G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations or an elimination of the starting point dependence. The dependence on the preceding mean-field calculation can be eliminated or reduced by employing some form of self-consistency as discussed in Section V or, as proposed only very recently, by replacing G0G_{0} by a renormalized singles Green’s function [257]. In this section we focus on the optimal choice of the starting point. The PBEh family of DFT functionals is convenient for this porpose, since one parameter (the amount of exact exchange α\alpha) governs the behavior of the starting point. Several schemes have been developed to find the optimal α\alpha value within the PBEh functional family [284, 408, 107, 64, 30]. We summarize them in the following.

IV.7.2 Consistent starting point scheme

Körzdörfer and Marom developed a consistent starting point (CSP) scheme that seeks a PBEh reference state (i.e. starting point) that best resembles the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} spectrum. Splitting both the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} self-energy and the starting hybrid functional into their respective exchange and correlation parts (see Equations (36) and (33)) allows us to rewrite the QP equation (Equation (26)) as follows [284, 350]

ϵs=\displaystyle\epsilon_{s}={} ϵs0+(1−α)​Δ​vsx+Δ​vsc\displaystyle\epsilon_{s}^{0}+(1-\alpha)\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{x}}+\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{c}} (72)
Δ​vsx:=\displaystyle\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{x}}:={} ⟨ϕs0|Σx−vxPBE|ϕs0⟩\displaystyle\langle\phi_{s}^{0}|\Sigma^{\mathrm{x}}-v_{\mathrm{x}}^{\mathrm{PBE}}|\phi_{s}^{0}\rangle (73)
Δ​vsc:=\displaystyle\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{c}}:={} ⟨ϕs0|Σc−vcPBE|ϕs0⟩.\displaystyle\langle\phi_{s}^{0}|\Sigma^{\mathrm{c}}-v_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{PBE}}|\phi_{s}^{0}\rangle. (74)

vxPBEv_{\mathrm{x}}^{\mathrm{PBE}} and vcPBEv_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{PBE}} are the exchange and correlation part of the PBE exchange-correlation potential, respectively. The optimal α\alpha is determined so that the shift between G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} and PBEh for the occupied states is approximately a constant kk

Δ​vsc+(1−α)​Δ​vsx≈k,s∈occ.\displaystyle\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{c}}+(1-\alpha)\Delta v_{s}^{\text{x}}\approx k,\quad s\in\text{occ}. (75)

If Equation (75) is satisfied, the positions of the PBEh orbital energies relative to each other are as close as possible to the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} energies. In this case, the QP correction amounts to a rigid shift of the PBEh spectrum. The value of α\alpha for which Equation (75) is satisfied yields the optimal starting point in the CSP scheme. If the PBEh and the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@PBEh spectrum matched perfectly, the constant kk would be zero. However, in general it is not possible to find a starting point whose spectrum matches the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} spectrum exactly.

For a given guess of α\alpha, Δ​vsx\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{x}} and Δ​vsc\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{c}} are calculated according to Equations (73) and (74). Δ​vsc\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{c}} is plotted as a function of Δ​vsx\Delta v_{s}^{\mathrm{x}} for a set of occupied states ss as data points, see Figure 19. A straight line fit determines a new α\alpha which is used to calculate new DFT eigenvalues and orbitals from PBEh(OPENαnew)\alpha_{\textnormal{new}}). From the new eigenvalues and orbitals, a new self-energy is calculated and Equations (73) and (74) are reassessed. This procedure is continued until the α\alpha of the linear fit equals the initial α\alpha. Then the optimal α\alpha has been found.

By construction, the PBEh(α\alpha) eigenvalues are now, up to the rigid shift kk, consistent with the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} spectrum. Typical CSP α\alpha values lie in the range of 0.25−0.300.25-0.30. The CSP scheme has been tested on several organic molecules that are used in organic electronics and yields good agreement with photoemission spectra in all cases [284, 285, 350].

IV.7.3 Deviation from the straight line scheme

A physically more rigorously motivated optimization scheme is based on the deviation from the straight line error (DSLE) [107]. In 1982, Perdew and co-workers showed that the total energy EE of any many-electron system should change linearly when varying the electron number continuously from NN to N−1N-1 electrons [404],

E⁡(f)=(1−f)​E​(N−1)+f​E​(N)f∈[0,1].E(f)=(1-f)E(N-1)+fE(N)\qquad f\in[0,1]. (76)

The function E⁡(f)E(f) is a piecewise linear function of the occupation number ff, with cusps at every integer value of ff, see Figure 20. Standard DFT functionals, however, violate this piecewise linearity condition and yield energies that deviate from the straight line at fractional occupation numbers ff [371, 474, 290]. The straight-line condition applies not only to DFT, but to any total energy method (we will address G​WGW total energies in Section X). Therefore, we can use the DSLE to find an optimal starting point for G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}.

The slope of the total energy as a function of occupation gives the Kohn-Sham eigenvalue or, in the G​WGW case, the quasiparticle excitation energy for a given electron number,

∂E∂f|f=1=E⁡(N)−E⁡(N−1)=\displaystyle\frac{\partial E}{\partial f}\bigg|_{f=1}=E(N)-E(N-1)={} ϵHOMO,N\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm HOMO,N} (77)
∂E∂f|f=0=E⁡(N)−E⁡(N−1)=\displaystyle\frac{\partial E}{\partial f}\bigg|_{f=0}=E(N)-E(N-1)={} ϵLUMO,N−1,\displaystyle\epsilon_{\rm LUMO,N-1}, (78)

where ϵHOMO,N\epsilon_{\rm HOMO,N} is the QP energy of the HOMO for the neutral system (NN). ϵLUMO,N−1\epsilon_{\rm LUMO,N-1} denotes the QP energy of the lowest unoccupied orbital (LUMO) for the charged system (N−1N-1). It is evident from Equation (77) and (78) that the slopes must be identical for f=0f=0 and f=1f=1 in an exact theory. In other words, a necessary condition for piecewise linearity is that the energy for removing an electron from the neutral system equals the energy for adding an electron to the positively charge system, i.e., the IP for the neutral systems and the electron affinity (EA) of the charged system should be equal. The difference

ΔDSLE\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{DSLE}} =EALUMO​(N−1)−IPHOMO​(N)\displaystyle=\text{EA}_{\text{LUMO}}(N-1)-\text{IP}_{\text{HOMO}}(N) (79)
=−ϵLUMO,N-1+ϵHOMO,N\displaystyle=-\epsilon_{\text{LUMO,N-1}}+\epsilon_{\text{HOMO,N}} (80)

should thus be zero and if it is not zero it quantifies the deviation from the straight line error ΔDSLE\Delta_{\text{DSLE}}.

The idea is now to find a PBEh starting point for which G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@PBEh minimizes ΔDLSE\Delta_{\text{DLSE}}. The optimal α\alpha value for PBEh can be found by the following procedure: We select a set of PBEh functionals with α\alpha values between 0 and 1. Then two G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations are performed for each starting point. One for the neutral system that yields ϵHOMO,N\epsilon_{\text{HOMO,N}} and a second one for the cation to obtain ϵLUMO,N-1\epsilon_{\text{LUMO,N-1}}. Following Equation (80), we calculate the difference between these two energies to estimate the deviation from the straight line condition. The PBEh(α\alpha) functional that yields the smallest ΔDSLE\Delta_{\text{DSLE}} will be the optimal starting point.

This DSLE scheme has been tested for small molecular systems, where it has been shown that the optimal α\alpha values are distributed around 0.35−0.400.35-0.40 for the first IP [107, 82]. The reported deviation from the CCSD(T) reference is smaller than 0.2 eV [82]. The drawback of the DSLE scheme is that the optimization is restricted to the HOMO. For other states, the straight line condition could still be formulated, but the corresponding G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations could not be performed because the electron occupation function would no longer correspond to an equilibrium distribution (see Section XI.3 for G​WGW calculations out of equilibrium). If we removed an electron from a lower lying occupied state, the sums over occupied and virtual orbitals in the polarizability χ0\chi_{0} would no longer be rigorously defined, i.e. the energy differences in the denominator in Equation (32) would exhibit the wrong sign.

IV.7.4 IP-theorem schemes

Several other schemes were developed that are, in spirit, similar to the CSP and DSLE optimization approaches, but are explicitly based on the ionization potential (IP) theorem. The latter states that in exact DFT the negative of the KS orbital can be strictly assigned to the first ionization potential IPHOMO\text{IP}_{\text{HOMO}} [13, 319]

IPHOMO=−ϵHOMOKS.\text{IP}_{\text{HOMO}}=-\epsilon_{\text{HOMO}}^{\text{KS}}. (81)

This statement is not true for any other KS state and not valid for approximate DFT functionals. Atalla et al. proposed a scheme that exploits the IP-theorem and minimizes the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} correction for the HOMO level with respect to the amount of exact exchange α\alpha in a PBEh starting point [30],

Δ​vHOMOc+(1−α)​Δ​vHOMOx=0.\displaystyle\Delta v_{\text{HOMO}}^{\mathrm{c}}+(1-\alpha)\Delta v_{\text{HOMO}}^{\text{x}}=0. (82)

This approach is similar to the CSP scheme in Equation (75). The difference is that we find the PBEh functional whose HOMO energy matches that of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@PBEh for the same α\alpha, whereas CSP looks for the closest spectral match between PBEh and G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@PBEh. HOMO excitations obtained from this IP-theorem-tuned scheme agree reasonably well with CCSD(T) reference data [64], but are not expected to reproduce the whole excitation spectrum properly [30]. They generally yield large α\alphas (around 0.8) and produce HOMOs and HOMO-LUMO gaps that are too large (i.e. under-screened).

Finding a PBEh(α\alpha) functional that fulfills the IP-theorem by enforcing consistency with the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} spectrum is one option. An alternative approach is to IP tune the hybrid functionals themselves [64] by minimizing

ΔIP=|ϵHOMOKS​(α)−(E⁡(N,α)−E⁡(N−1,α))|\Delta_{\text{IP}}=\left|\epsilon_{\text{HOMO}}^{\text{KS}}(\alpha)-(E(N,\alpha)-E(N-1,\alpha))\right| (83)

with respect to α\alpha. These IP-tuned hybrids already give accurate KS-HOMO energies. Recent benchmark studies for molecular systems showed that G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} corrections on top of ΔIP\Delta_{\text{IP}}-tuned functionals provide spectral properties in good agreement with experiment for the whole excitation spectrum [431, 130, 163, 164, 276, 64]. In particular, EAs are well reproduced with mean-average deviation (MADs) <0.2<0.2 eV from CCSD(T) references, while the MAD reported for IPHOMO{}_{\text{HOMO}} is 0.1 eV [276].

IV.8 Computational complexity and cost

Of all the G​WGW schemes described in this review, G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} is the computationally most efficient one. Only the diagonal elements of the self-energy are needed and the Green’s function that enters is always G0G_{0}. The fully interacting GG, on the contrary, depends on the full self-energy and can only be obtained by iterating Dyson’s equation G=G0+G0​Σ​GG=G_{0}+G_{0}\Sigma G.

The computational complexity of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} depends on the frequency integration method and design of the algorithm. The most accurate integration technique, the fully-analytic approach, requires the solution of the full Casida equations, which is an 𝒪⁡(N6)\mathcal{O}(N^{6}) step with respect to the system size NN, see Section IV.3.5. In the canonical implementation, the computational cost is reduced to 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}). Different implementations with N4N^{4} complexity have been developed employing a variety of numerical techniques specific for the respective basis set [508, 57, 114, 437, 194, 586]. For example, the 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}) algorithm proposed by Ren et al. employs localized basis functions and the AC method [437]. The computational and memory costs for the four-center electron repulsion integrals (4c-ERIs) are reduced by refactoring the latter in two- and three-center Coulomb integrals using a resolution-of-the-identity (RI) approach with a so-called Coulomb metric [567]. The accuracy of this algorithm has been validated for valence excitations and EAs by comparing to the fully analytic approach [492]. However, for core states it was recently shown that AC fails and that CD is required [189]. The computational complexity of CD remains unchanged for valence states, but increases to 𝒪⁡(N5)\mathcal{O}(N^{5}) for the deep states.

The 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}) scaling and overall cost of canonical G​WGW implementations restricts the tractable system size and prohibits the study of many systems that are relevant in the chemistry and physics community, such as solid-liquid interfaces, molecules in solution, complex alloys, nanostructures or hybrid interfaces, that require large simulation cells with hundreds to thousands of atoms. To make G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations feasible for larger systems, the scaling and computational complexity have been scrutinized. Developments have proceeded in two directions: 1) reducing the prefactor, i.e. the overall computational cost at 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}) scaling, or 2) reducing the scaling.

The prefactor has been reduced by low-rank approximations of χ0\chi_{0}, which map χ0\chi_{0} onto a smaller basis [590, 591, 194, 110, 565]. Another approach is the elimination of the sum over empty orbitals in χ0\chi_{0} and in G0G_{0} [194, 566, 303, 181, 406] by solving the Sternheimer equation [530], which we discussed in Section IV.6. Others developed techniques to reduce the number of unoccupied states [73, 71]. The prefactor can also be controlled by choosing an optimal basis set for the respective system under study. In the last years, several algorithms for localized basis sets have been developed [57, 264, 437, 495, 586, 76]. These basis sets are generally smaller than traditional plane wave basis sets and considerably more efficient for molecules. However, the development of reliable G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} algorithm for periodic systems based on localized basis sets is still underway [588].

The reduction of the exponent to 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) complexity has been addressed in different ways. Foerster et al. developed a cubic-scaling G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} algorithm using Gaussian basis sets and exploiting locality in the electronic structure, albeit with a high prefactor [148]. Recently, two cubic-scaling algorithms have been devised [332, 587], which are both variants of the 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) G​WGW space time method [466]. The key step of these algorithms is the computation of the irreducible polarizability in imaginary time, χ0​(i​t)=−i​G0​(i​t)​G0​(−i​t)\chi_{0}(it)=-iG_{0}(it)G_{0}(-it) and the subsequent transformation to imaginary frequencies i​ωi\omega. The time-ordered non-interacting Green’s function in imaginary time is given by

G0​(𝐫,𝐫′,i​t)={i∑ioccϕi0(𝐫)ϕi0∗(𝐫′)exp(−ϵi0t),t<0,−i∑avirtϕa0(𝐫)ϕa0∗(𝐫′)exp(−ϵa0t),t>0.\displaystyle\begin{split}G_{0}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},it)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}i\sum\limits_{i}^{\text{occ}}\phi_{i}^{0}({\bf r})\phi_{i}^{0*}({\bf r^{\prime}})\exp(-\epsilon_{i}^{0}t)\,,&t<0\,,\\[5.0pt] -i\sum\limits_{a}^{\text{virt}}\phi_{a}^{0}({\bf r})\phi_{a}^{0*}({\bf r^{\prime}})\exp(-\epsilon_{a}^{0}t)\,,&t>0\,.\end{array}\right.\end{split} (84)

Inserting G0​(i​t)G_{0}(it), the summation over occupied and virtual states is now decoupled in χ0​(i​t)\chi_{0}(it) and can be performed separately, which is fundamental for the reduction to 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) complexity.

Liu et al. based their cubic-scaling algorithm on a plane wave basis set in combination with a PAW scheme and reported a linear-scaling with the number of 𝐤\mathbf{k} points used to sample the Brillouin zone [332]. In combination, this paves the way for G​WGW calculations of large periodic systems. Wilhelm et al. employed a Gaussian basis set and exploited sparse matrix algebra by using an overlap metric for the RI approximation (RI-SVS) to refactor the 4c-ERIs [567]. The step with the largest prefactor, the computation of χ0\chi_{0}, is reduced from 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}) to 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) in this algorithm, while the other operations scale with N3N^{3}. A comparison between the 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}) algorithm developed by Ren et al. [437] and the low-scaling algorithm is shown in Figure 21 for graphene nanoribbons. The canonical algorithm is restricted to system sizes of less than 500 atoms, while systems with more than 1600 atoms can be addressed with the low-scaling implementation. These are some of the largest G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations with high accuracy and full-frequency integration reported so far. The mean absolute deviation with respect to the canonical reference implementation in FHI-aims [437] is less than 35 meV for the G​WGW100 test set [587], which is discussed more in detail in Section IX.3.

An actual linear scaling algorithm was devised within the framework of stochastic G​WGW[381] and applied to silicon clusters with 1000 atoms. However, the verification of its general reliability is still the subject of ongoing research [570].

IV.9 Practical guidelines

In summary, the following points should be considered when conducting G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations:

  1. 1.

    Frequency integration technique
    A sufficiently accurate method for the frequency integration of Equation(27) has to be chosen. The required precision depends on the systems and in particular on the states of interest, see Section IV.3.

  2. 2.

    Basis set choice
    The decision should be guided by the system of interest. Localized basis sets are generally more efficient for finite systems, while plane wave G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} codes are currently superior for extended systems (see detailed discussion in Section IV.4).

  3. 3.

    Basis set convergence
    G​WGW     calculations have to be carefully converged with respect to basis set size. Extrapolation procedures to the complete basis set limits might be required as demonstrated in Section IV.5.

  4. 4.

    Starting point
    The QP energies depend strongly on the functional of the preceding DFT calculation as shown in Section IV.7. While for solid state systems GGA functionals are often suitable starting points (see also Section VI), hybrid functionals perform better for molecules. A judicious choice of the starting point is necessary.

  5. 5.

    Convergence of technical parameters
    G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}     calculations usually require the convergence of a few additional parameters, which are strongly implementation dependent. Such a parameter is, e.g., the size of the integration grid for the imaginary frequency terms in the CD and AC approach. G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} practitioners should always carefully check their G​WGW code to ensue the robustness and convergence of all available settings and parameters

The G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} approximation provides computationally efficient access to the whole QP spectrum. Despite these appealing features G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} has certain drawbacks. The most severe is the dependence on the starting point discussed in Section IV.7. Furthermore, the ground state energy and density cannot be computed. In Sections V and X, we will show how these drawbacks can be overcome.

V Beyond 𝑮𝟎​𝑾𝟎\bm{G_{0}W_{0}}: self-consistency schemes

V.1 Fully self-consistent 𝑮​𝑾\bm{GW}

To go beyond G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, one must include some level of self-consistency in Hedin’s G​WGW equations. The conceptually purest approach to G​WGW is to perform full self-consistency in the G​WGW equations, denoted as scG​WGW. It is also the most expensive. As introduced in Section III, all four quantities are iterated until self-consistency in the Green’s function is achieved. Until now, self-consistent G​WGW is the rarest form of G​WGW for reasons of computational expense and conceptual controversy (see below), although that is slowly changing.

The first scG​WGW calculation was performed for the homogeneous electron gas (HEG) by 234, after the same authors had previously applied partial self-consistency (scG​W0GW_{0}) [39]. Later studies were extended to the 2D HEG [169]. scG​WGW deteriorates the spectral properties of the HEG compared to G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}. This deterioration manifests itself in a quasiparticle bandwidth that is larger than the free electron one and a broad and featureless satellite spectrum. Both results contradict experimental evidence for alkali metals which are HEG-like [39]. Also, band gaps of simple semiconductors are greatly overestimated by scG​WGW [490, 198]. scG​WGW calculations for atoms [525] and molecules [471, 87, 351, 89, 86] show improvements over G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} for the first ionization energies and transport properties [531] of finite systems. With regard to the whole spectrum, however, scG​WGW is usually outperformed by G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} with a judicious starting-point choice [351, 86, 276].

scG​WGW is computationally more demanding than G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} because the full Green’s function must be stored and calculated [86], increasing memory and computation requirements. In G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, the full Green’s function is only required in 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) schemes (see Section IV.8). Other implementations make use of the fact that intermediate quantities can be expressed in terms of the mean-field wave functions and eigenvalues, which reduces the computational complexity (see Section IV.1). Furthermore, iterations of the G​WGW equations for scG​WGW are expensive. χ0\chi_{0}, WW, and Σ\Sigma must be computed at each iteration, with a potentially high computational time for even a single evaluation of Σ\Sigma.

Conceptually, the additional self-consistency in the Green’s function adds more reducible diagrams compared to G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, as Figure 22 illustrates. In G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, the bare Coulomb interaction is screened by a series of sequentially interacting electron-hole pairs, or “bubbles.” In scG​WGW, this structure is preserved, but the bubbles are now composed of interacting Green’s function lines instead of non-interacting G0G_{0} lines. This effect is a general feature of iterating Green’s function diagrams. By iterating diagrams for a given approximation, initial G0G_{0} lines at internal times become interacting GG lines. Already after the first iteration of the cycle (G1G_{1} in Figure 22), the Green’s function contains sequential self-energy insertions.

Let us look more closely at how this occurs. Recall from Equation (17) that Dyson’s equation is

G⁡(1,2)\displaystyle G(1,2) =G0​(1,2)\displaystyle=G_{0}(1,2) (85)
+∫G0(1,3)Σ(3,4)G(4,2)d(3,4).\displaystyle+\int G_{0}(1,3)\Sigma(3,4)G(4,2)d(3,4).

The first guess at the full GG, labeled G1G_{1}, would then be

G1​(1,2)\displaystyle G_{1}(1,2) =G0​(1,2)\displaystyle=G_{0}(1,2) (86)
+∫G0(1,3)Σ0(3,4)G1(4,2)d(3,4),\displaystyle+\int G_{0}(1,3)\Sigma_{0}(3,4)G_{1}(4,2)d(3,4),

where we have inserted G1​(4,2)G_{1}(4,2) in place of G⁡(4,2)G(4,2) on the right-hand-side (RHS). Σ0\Sigma_{0} is the first estimate to the self-energy, evaluated with G0G_{0} wherever GG lines enter the self-energy diagram. G1G_{1} appears on both sides of Equation (86) −- by replacing G1​(4,2)G_{1}(4,2) on the RHS with the entire RHS, one can generate a reducible diagram for G1G_{1} that is 𝒪⁡(Σ02)\mathcal{O}(\Sigma_{0}^{2}). At this point, the series for G1G_{1} contains three parts: G0G_{0}, a term of order 𝒪⁡(Σ0)\mathcal{O}(\Sigma_{0}), and a term of order 𝒪⁡(Σ02)\mathcal{O}(\Sigma_{0}^{2}). These contributions to G1G_{1} are shown in Figure 22. By further iterating G1G_{1} on the RHS, one can generate all reducible diagrams which contribute to G1G_{1}. Despite the infinite number of reducible diagrams generated by this prescription, G1G_{1} is still computed only with the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} self-energy because we have not updated Σ0\Sigma_{0}. This example also demonstrates why it is conceptually much simpler to work only with the irreducible self-energy and avoid this infinite, reducible series. Indeed, iterating Equation (86) to find G1G_{1} while keeping Σ0\Sigma_{0} fixed is equivalent to generating the entire reducible series for G1G_{1}.

In scG​WGW, the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation of Σ0\Sigma_{0} to build G1G_{1} is only the first step. Next, we update Σ0\Sigma_{0} to Σ1\Sigma_{1} by inserting G1G_{1} into the self-energy diagram. The diagram contains one obvious GG line (Σ=i​G​W\Sigma=iGW), but contains more that are hidden in the polarisability entering WW. By updating the polarisability with G1G_{1} in place of G0G_{0}, the diagrams contained in G1G_{1} enter the screened Coulomb interaction. Just as before, we can generate all reducible diagrams contributing to the updated Green’s function (G2G_{2}) by iterating the Dyson series

G2​(1,2)\displaystyle G_{2}(1,2) =G0​(1,2)\displaystyle=G_{0}(1,2) (87)
+∫G0(1,3)Σ1(3,4)G2(4,2)d(3,4)\displaystyle+\int G_{0}(1,3)\Sigma_{1}(3,4)G_{2}(4,2)d(3,4)

for a fixed Σ1\Sigma_{1}. Continuing to update Σ\Sigma and iterate GG introduces more and more reducible diagrams. The solution is self-consistent when GG entering Σ\Sigma is the same as GG from iterating Dyson’s equation.

In real scG​WGW calculations, the procedure is slightly different. GG and Σ\Sigma are updated together instead of iterating to find Gi+1G_{i+1} at a fixed Σi\Sigma_{i}. After the first iteration of Equation (86), the updated −- but not yet self-consistent −- G1G_{1} is inserted into Σ\Sigma. This way, Σ\Sigma is updated at each iteration along with GG. The combined iterations are much more efficient because GG and Σ\Sigma converge together. Bear in mind that the efficient method of updating GG and Σ\Sigma at each step does not form the same easy-to-interpret series for G1G_{1} as in Figure 22. Note that even after one iteration to find GG and Σ\Sigma, we would already go beyond G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}.

Based on Figure 22, the fully dressed Green’s function and screened Coulomb interaction in scG​WGW can be interpreted as double renormalisations of G0G_{0} and W0W_{0} through the two Dyson’s equations in the G​WGW equations. However, the third Dyson equation that the vertex function (Equation (142)) would introduce is missing from the G​WGW equations. The absence of the vertex function has important consequences. Figure 23 shows two of the reducible diagrams that enter WW in scG​WGW, but that are not present in W0W_{0}. The diagram on the left shows the polarisation bubble with the insertion of one interaction, or scattering event, in each arch. It is part of a series of sequential scattering events and builds additional interactions into the screened Coulomb interaction. The other diagram, however, is problematic. After the creation of the first electron-hole pair, both the electron and the hole interact with a new electron-hole pair. The two new electron-hole pairs are composed of the same Green’s function lines as the initial electron-hole pair, even though the initial pair still exists. Therefore, the two later pairs do not account for the fact that the initial electron-hole pair has already been created −- they should somehow omit the pair already created. The electron (or hole) thus interacts or correlates with itself. The problems that have been identified99 9 It has also been pointed out that the exact WW from RPA does not satisfy the f-sum rule. for scG​WGW can be attributed to diagrams like the one on the RHS of Figure 23 [468].

We would also like to briefly comment on partial self-consistency in the Green’s function. The above discussion points to the screened Coulomb interaction as the major source of imbalance between self-consistency and the missing vertex corrections. This imbalance can be partially fixed by keeping WW fixed at the W0W_{0} level and iterating only the Green’s function to self-consistency (scG​W0GW_{0}). This is shown schematically in Figure 24. This approximation is partially motivated by a “best GG, best WW” philosophy that can improve agreement with experiment in certain situations.

Before leaving the discussion of self-consistent G​WGW, we introduce one of the most technical and modern aspects of Green’s function theory being researched: the existence of multiple solutions for GG from a single Dyson equation [546]. This issue has been studied in detail for the zero-dimensional one-point model (OPM) [547, 47, 307] and has been produced numerically [289, 203, 571]. In the analytic OPM, there exist two interacting GG which can be mapped from the same G0G_{0} [526, 469]. One of these solutions is the physical GG for all values of interaction strength. Here, the physical solution is characterized by a smooth connection to G0G_{0}, unlike the unphysical solution for GG which diverges at zero interaction strength. The reverse map, from GG to G0G_{0}, has two solutions for G0G_{0} which must be disentangled at a certain interaction strength. At this point, the physical G0G_{0} switches between the two solutions, so that solving the problem for all interaction strengths requires switching solution methods at this point. Otherwise, one would obtain a physical G0G_{0} for some interaction strengths and an unphysical G0G_{0} for others. In the OPM, this is now understood. However, it is not well understood if or how this same phenomenon emerges in more realistic systems.

V.2 Eigenvalue self-consistency and level alignment

There are a few strategies to reduce the expense of scG​WGW while still including more physics than G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}. The simplest form of performing approximate self-consistency in G​WGW is to iterate in the eigenvalues (evG​WGW). After completion of the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} loop, the real parts of the quasiparticle energies obtained from Equation (26) or (38) are reinserted into the non-interacting Green’s function G0G_{0} (Equation (28)) in place of the starting eigenvalues. Through G0G_{0}, the change in eigenvalues permeates through W0W_{0} to the self-energy and eventually to the quasiparticle energies (evG​WGW). After iterating until the input quantities equal the output, the equations are self-consistent in the eigenvalues.

Eigenvalue self-consistency was already proposed in the first G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation for real materials [243] and has since been applied frequently (see e.g. 509 for a more in-depth analysis). However, since only the real part of the quasiparticle energies is used and the wave functions are not updated self-consistently, the starting point dependence cannot be eliminated entirely. For example, a study for azabenzenes demonstrates that although the starting point dependence is reduced from 1.4 eV in G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, it cannot be lowered beyond 0.4 eV [351].

For molecular systems, it has been shown that eigenvalue self-consistency improves the HOMO-LUMO gaps, which are then in good agreement with experiment [57, 586]. However, examining the entire spectrum reveals that evG​WGW does not lead to consistent improvements over G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}. The evG​WGW spectra are overly stretched with respect to the experimental spectra, such that large deviations (on the order of 1 eV) from experiment occur for lower lying states. Moreover, for most systems, the orbital ordering deviates from experimental observations [351]. This is in line with observations for semiconductors and insulators, that find band gaps to be considerably overestimated in evG​WGW [509]. The reason for this overestimation in solids lies in the fact that the insertion of the quasiparticle energies into the screened Coulomb interaction leads to an underscreening, which should be compensated by the missing vertex corrections, as discussed previously.

Just as scG​W0GW_{0} ameliorates problems in self-consistent G​WGW, one can perform eigenvalue self-consistency only in GG to circumvent underscreening errors. Iterating the eigenvalues in only GG produces an evG​W0GW_{0} scheme that gives band gaps in good agreement with experiment [509]. However, for open shell systems, it was observed that eigenvalue self-consistency in GG strongly affects the calculated multiplet splittings [329].

The effect of eigenvalue self-consistency in GG on the self-energy is demonstrated in Figure 25 for an evG​W0GW_{0} calculation. Compared to G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, the structure of the self-energy is almost identical, but shifted to lower energies. The Green’s function in the eigenvalue self-consistent G​W0GW_{0} scheme is given by

Gevσ​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=∑mϕm​σ0(𝐫)ϕm​σ0∗(𝐫′)ω−ϵm​σ−i​η​sgn⁡(EF−ϵm​σ)G_{\textnormal{ev}}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\omega)=\sum_{m}\frac{\phi_{m\sigma}^{0}(\mathbf{r})\phi_{m\sigma}^{0*}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})}{\omega-\epsilon_{m\sigma}-i\eta\sgn(E_{\rm F}-\epsilon_{m\sigma})} (88)

with

ϵm​σ\displaystyle\epsilon_{m\sigma} =ϵm​σ0+Δ​ϵm​σ\displaystyle=\epsilon_{m\sigma}^{0}+\Delta\epsilon_{m\sigma} (89)
Δ​ϵm​σ\displaystyle\Delta\epsilon_{m\sigma} =Σm​σ​(ϵm​σ)−vm​σMF.\displaystyle=\Sigma_{m\sigma}\left(\epsilon_{m\sigma}\right)-v^{\rm MF}_{m\sigma}. (90)

Inserting the G​WGW corrections Δ​ϵm​σ\Delta\epsilon_{m\sigma} into the Green’s function results in a shift of the poles in the self-energy, see Equation (52). On the real axis, the poles of Σsc\Sigma_{s}^{c} are located at ωi​σn=ϵi​σ0+Δ​ϵi​σ−Ωn​σ\omega_{i\sigma}^{n}=\epsilon_{i\sigma}^{0}+\Delta\epsilon_{i\sigma}-\Omega_{n\sigma} and ωa​σn=ϵa​σ0+Δ​ϵa​σ+Ωn​σ\omega_{a\sigma}^{n}=\epsilon_{a\sigma}^{0}+\Delta\epsilon_{a\sigma}+\Omega_{n\sigma}, where ii indicates again occupied and aa virtual states. Starting from a GGA functional, the correction Δ​ϵm​σ\Delta\epsilon_{m\sigma} is negative for occupied and positive for virtual states. Compared to a G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} scheme, the poles ωi​σn\omega_{i\sigma}^{n} are now located at lower and the poles ωa​σn\omega_{a\sigma}^{n} at higher frequencies.

A simplified version of evG​W0GW_{0} was originally suggested by Hedin [217] and has been revisited a few times by others [218, 410, 355]. Instead of using an individual shift Δ​ϵm​σ\Delta\epsilon_{m\sigma} for each state mm, a global shift Δ​E\Delta E is employed:

GΔ​Eσ​(𝐫,𝐫′CLOSE,\displaystyle G_{\Delta E}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}, OPENω)=\displaystyle\omega)=
∑m\displaystyle\sum_{m} ϕm​σ0(𝐫)ϕm​σ0∗(𝐫′)ω−(ϵm​σ0+Δ​Eσ)−i​η​sgn⁡(EF−ϵm​σ0),\displaystyle\frac{\phi_{m\sigma}^{0}(\mathbf{r})\phi_{m\sigma}^{0*}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})}{\omega-(\epsilon_{m\sigma}^{0}+\Delta E_{\sigma})-i\eta\sgn(E_{\rm F}-\epsilon_{m\sigma}^{0})}, (91)

where G0σ​(ω−Δ​Eσ)=GΔ​Eσ​(ω)G^{\sigma}_{0}(\omega-\Delta E_{\sigma})=G_{\Delta E}^{\sigma}(\omega). The QP equation (Equation 26) then transforms into

ϵs​σ=ϵs​σ0+Σs​σ​(ϵs​σ−Δ​Eσ)−vs​σMF.\epsilon_{s\sigma}=\epsilon_{s\sigma}^{0}+\Sigma_{s\sigma}\left(\epsilon_{s\sigma}-\Delta E_{\sigma}\right)-v^{\rm MF}_{s\sigma}. (92)

For metals, the shift Δ​E\Delta E is chosen in such a way that the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} Fermi energy aligns with that of the starting point calculation, i.e. with the Fermi level of G0G_{0}. For systems with a energy gap, the highest occupied state is aligned, i.e., the valence band maximum for solids or the HOMO for finite systems. The latter is motivated by “DFT Koopman’s theorem”, which states that only the KS energy of the HOMO can be rigorously assigned to the ionization potential when starting from an exact DFT functional [13, 319]. In that case Δ​E\Delta E would be zero.

The shift can be determined by demanding self-consistency for the highest occupied state

ϵHOMO,σ=ϵHOMO,σ0+Δ​Eσ.\epsilon_{\rm HOMO,\sigma}=\epsilon_{\rm HOMO,\sigma}^{0}+\Delta E_{\sigma}. (93)

Inserting Equation (93) into Equation (92) yields the explicit expression

Δ​Eσ=ΣHOMO,σ​(ϵHOMO,σ0)−vHOMO,σMF.\Delta E_{\sigma}=\Sigma_{\rm HOMO,\sigma}\left(\epsilon_{\rm{HOMO},\sigma}^{0}\right)-v^{\rm MF}_{\rm HOMO,\sigma}. (94)

Adjusting the energy scale of G0σG_{0}^{\sigma} by Δ​E\Delta E translates to a rigid shift of the self-energy as shown in Figure 25. The results are very similar to evG​W0GW_{0} in the frequency range where the quasiparticle solution is expected.

The Δ​E\Delta E scheme is less frequently used for the calculation of quasiparticle energies than eigenvalue self-consistent schemes. However, it has been shown that it substantially improves satellite spectra [410]. The same holds for the evG​W0GW_{0} scheme, which has been employed to calculate satellite spectra of VO2 [173] and bulk sodium [609].

V.3 Self-consistency via a new ground state

Building on the idea of iterating in the quasiparticle energies, one can go one step further and also incorporate wave function changes. An elegant way to achieve this is to find the variationally best mean-field potential to a given self-energy [184, 186, 92, 481, 286]. This mean-field potential can then be used to generate new eigenvalues and eigenfunctions to construct a new G0G_{0} for the next iteration of the G​WGW cycle.

If the new potential is local, this iteration can be formalized exactly in the optimized effective potential (OEP) framework [92, 295], which is equivalent to the Sham-Schlüter equation [184, 186]. The OEP framework and the Sham-Schlüter equation only guarantee that the density generated by the local potential matches the G​WGW density. The eigenvalue spectrum of the local potential will not be the same as the G​WGW spectrum. For explicitly non-local potentials, no formally exact match between the G​WGW self-energy and the potential has been found because the self-energy is non-local and frequency dependent, while the constructed potential is non-local but static.

An approximate non-local potential can be found by introducing the G​WGW Hamiltonian h^G​W​(ω)=h^0+vH+ΣG​W​(ω)\hat{h}^{GW}(\omega)=\hat{h}^{0}+v_{\mathrm{H}}+\Sigma^{GW}(\omega). The mean-field Hamiltonian h^MF\hat{h}^{\text{MF}} that best reproduces the effects of ΣG​W\Sigma^{GW} is defined as h^MF=h^0+vH+vMF\hat{h}^{\mathrm{MF}}=\hat{h}^{0}+v_{\mathrm{H}}+v^{\mathrm{MF}}, see also Equations (22)-(24) for the definitions of the Hamiltonians. vMFv^{\mathrm{MF}} can then be obtained by minimizing ‖h^G​W−h^MF‖||\hat{h}^{GW}-\hat{h}^{\text{MF}}|| [481, 286]. An approximate minimization finally yields an analytic expression for the (static and Hermitian) mean-field potential [142, 481, 286]

vi​jMF=12​[[Re​Σ​(ϵi)]i​j+[Re​Σ​(ϵj)]i​j]v^{\text{MF}}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left[\mathrm{Re}\,\Sigma(\epsilon_{i})\right]_{ij}+\left[\mathrm{Re}\,\Sigma(\epsilon_{j})\right]_{ij}\right] (95)

where “Re\mathrm{Re}” signifies here the Hermitian part of Σ⁡(ϵk)\Sigma(\epsilon_{k})

[Re​Σ​(ϵk)]i​j=12​[Σ⁡(ϵk)+Σ​(ϵk)†]i​j.\left[\mathrm{Re}\,\Sigma(\epsilon_{k})\right]_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Sigma(\epsilon_{k})+\Sigma(\epsilon_{k})^{\dagger}\right]_{ij}. (96)

The quasiparticle energies for the Green’s function GG are then given by the self-consistent G0G_{0} that follows from vi​jMFv^{\text{MF}}_{ij} [481]. Satellites or the incoherent part of the spectra function are not captured by this approximation. This is why the scheme is commonly referred to as quasiparticle self-consistent G​WGW (QSG​WGW). Reports of a starting point dependence for metal oxides [326, 245] have not yet been reproduced by other groups with a different implementation. In general, the QSG​WGW scheme converges to a unique solution.

An alternative definition for a non-local mean-field potential is given by the static Coulomb hole plus screened exchange (COHSEX) approximation to G​WGW [217, 220]:

vσMF,COHSEX​(𝐫,𝐫′)=ΣσCOH​(𝐫,𝐫′)+ΣσSEX​(𝐫,𝐫′).v_{\sigma}^{\text{MF,COHSEX}}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})=\Sigma^{\rm COH}_{\sigma}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})+\Sigma^{\rm SEX}_{\sigma}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}}). (97)

The screened exchange (SEX) term is defined in analogy to the exact-exchange self-energy in Equation (36) but with the statically screened Coulomb interaction instead of the bare one

ΣσSEX(𝐫,𝐫′)=−∑ioccϕσ​i(𝐫)ϕσ​i∗(𝐫′)W(𝐫,𝐫′,ω=0),\Sigma^{\rm SEX}_{\sigma}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})=-\sum_{i}^{\rm occ}\phi_{\sigma i}({\bf r})\phi_{\sigma i}^{*}({\bf r^{\prime}})W({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega=0)\,, (98)

where ϕσ​i\phi_{\sigma i} are eigenfunctions of the COHSEX mean-field Hamiltonian. The static Coulomb hole (COH) term, on the other hand, becomes local in space

ΣσCOH​(𝐫,𝐫′)=δ⁡(𝐫−𝐫′)​[W⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω=0)−v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)].\Sigma^{\rm COH}_{\sigma}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})=\delta({\bf r}-{\bf r^{\prime}})\left[W({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega=0)-v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})\right]\,. (99)

The statically screened Coulomb interaction W⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω=0)W({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}},\omega=0), which enters in Equations (98) and (99), is obtained by inserting the COHSEX eigevalues and eigenfunctions in Equations (29)-(32) for ω=0\displaystyle{\omega=0}. Like in QSGW, vσMF,COHSEX​(𝐫,𝐫′)v_{\sigma}^{\text{MF,COHSEX}}({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}}) produces new eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, which yield a new self-energy. The COHSEX equation can then be iterated until self-consistency is achieved.

COHSEX can also serve as an improved starting point compared to KS-DFT for a perturbative G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation. After completing a COHSEX calculation, one can use the self-consistent COHSEX eigenvalues and wave functions for a perturbative G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation with the full, dynamical WW. In the case of VO2 [171], G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@LDA fails to open the band gap. On the other hand, G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@COHSEX opens a band gap, in agreement with experiment. The improved COHSEX starting point is especially important for materials with localized electrons [8]. When comparing to benchmark coupled cluster data on organic molecules, the COHSEX starting point decreases the mean absolute error of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} compared to G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@PBE [276]. In Ge under pressure, G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@COHSEX predicts a direct gap at the Γ\Gamma point while G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@LDA predicts band overlap [248].

Self-consistency in G​WGW is a topic that is still being researched. While the results from true self-consistent G​WGW are usually in worse agreement with experiment than G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} [509, 490, 198], studies of self-consistency are still necessary to advance the field. We can learn about shortcomings of the theory or assess challenging materials. Most importantly, self-consistent G​WGW implementations are a necessary foundation to go beyond G​WGW in the future, as discussed in Section XI.

VI Solids

Solids were the first testbed of G​WGW theory in real materials. The basic quantity to compute in solids is the band structure. Unlike in molecules with single-particle states given by molecular orbitals, single particles in solids occupy Bloch waves, defined in Equation (54) and indexed by their wave vector 𝐤\mathbf{k}. Diagonalizing the Hamiltonian at each 𝐤\mathbf{k} gives its own set of single-particle eigenvalues. One can conveniently visualize the eigenvalues at different 𝐤\mathbf{k}-points by varying 𝐤\mathbf{k} continuously along some path, placed on the x-axis, and plotting the eigenvalues on the y-axis. Eigenvalues change continuously with 𝐤\mathbf{k}, forming separate bands of states. The collection of single-particle states in bands is similar to the grouping of different combinations of bonding and anti-bonding states in molecules or polymers. Quasiparticle Hamiltonians are also 𝐤\mathbf{k}-dependent, and energies at all 𝐤\mathbf{k} form a band structure which can be compared to angle resolved PES and IPES spectra as the incident momentum is varied (see Figure 2).

Computing quasiparticle band structures with G​WGW gives the quasiparticle band gap, analogous to the HOMO-LUMO gap in molecules. The first G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations for real materials [242, 243, 539, 540] focused on semiconductors (Si, Ge) and insulators (diamond, LiCl). G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations in semiconductors and insulators give a uniform improvement in band gap over estimates with either Hartree-Fock or Kohn-Sham eigenvalues, as shown in Figure 26(a). This improvement was the first major success of the G​WGW theory.

The success of G​WGW applied to semiconductors continued with other studies [184, 186, 185, 187, 58]. Many common semiconductors lack semicore states and are well described by pseudopotentials (see Section IV.4.4). These factors reduce the computational complexity for G​WGW calculations and made early, realistic G​WGW calculations of semiconductors feasible. Screening in simple semiconductors can also be approximated by model dielectric functions like plasmon-pole models (see Sec. IV.3.1), eliminating the need for a numerical evaluation of the self-energy integral.

It was later realized that semicore dd-electrons in semiconductors such as GaN, ZnO, ZnS, ZnSe or CdS [457, 459, 461] and metals such as Cu [349] and Au [426] have a strong influence on G​WGW calculations. Due to the strong overlap of the atomic dd functions with the atomic ss and pp functions in the same shell, the exchange self-energy is very sensitive to the inclusion of semicore states. If only the semicore dd states are explicitly included as valence state in the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation, while the ss and pp states in the same shell are frozen in the core of a pseudopotential, the subsequent G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation will produce an incorrect band gap [457]. This problem can be solved by explicitly including the entire shell as valence in the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculation [457, 339, 553, 147], by using exact-exchange pseudopotentials and exact-exchange starting points [445, 419, 446] or by all-electron calculations [157, 508, 155, 201, 250].

VI.1 Band gaps

Figure 26(a) shows the quasiparticle band gap computed with G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} and evG​W0GW_{0} with a modern all-electron LAPW code [250] for several different semiconductors and insulators. Perfect agreement between theory and experiment would place all data points on the dashed blue line. Generally, Kohn-Sham eigenvalues based on a multiplicative (local or semi-local) exchange-correlation potential (here PBE) underestimate the band gap and Hartree-Fock eigenvalues overestimate (not shown in Figure 26). Eigenvalue self-consistency (evG​W0GW_{0}) improves the agreement with experiment even further than G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}, when starting from a local or semi-local DFT calculation.

Figure 26(b) compares band gaps computed with different self-consistency schemes [198] for a different set of semiconductors and insulators than in panel (a). G0​W0G_{0}W_{0}@PBE again provides good agreement with experiment (i.e. the red squares are close to the diagonal). Van Schilfgaarde’s QSGW scheme [481] and fully self-consistent G​WGW calculations consistently overestimate band gaps.

With the predictive accuracy of G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} band gaps validated, we provide a few examples in which G​WGW calculations helped to resolve band gap controversies. One case is InN. In the early 2000s, alloys of GaN and InN were revolutionizing light-emitting diode (LED) technology. However, the band gap of InN was believed to be almost 2 eV [79], which would have severely limited the usefulness of InGaN alloys to tune the emission of LEDs. Through G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations and more refined experiments, the real value of the InN band gap was found to be 0.7 eV [41, 161, 447], paving the way for the LEDs we know today. Another example is hybrid perovskites that have triggered a new boom in the emergent photovoltaic materials field. The prototypical material is methylammonium lead triiodide (CH3NH3PbI3 or in short MAPI). Unusually, local or semi-local DFT calculations already predict a band gap in good agreement with measurements, which had caused initial confusion in the field. However, when spin-orbit effects, which are particularly strong in this materials class, are incorporated in the DFT calculations, the band gap becomes significantly underestimated again. G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} and QSGW calculations that include spin-orbit effects then predict the correct band gap [564, 68].

Finally, we consider high pressure physics. At high pressures (∼100\sim 100 GPa), many materials experience band gap closure and transition from an insulator to a metal. There can also be many competing structural phases, each with their own metallization pressure, that are difficult to disentangle in experiments. G​WGW is an excellent tool to theoretically predict the metallization pressure for different structural phases and help interpret experimental results [562, 423, 256, 603, 268]. Solid hydrogen is a noteworthy example of metallization at high pressure, first predicted in 1935 [585]. The metallic hydrogen puzzle is an exceptionally difficult one that is still not fully understood, but G​WGW calculations help corroborate experimental measurements and support the existence of certain structural phases [309, 363, 123].

VI.2 Band structures and band parameters

With G​WGW, one can compute much more than only the band gap of a solid. A typical band structure computed with G​WGW is shown in Figure 27 for ZnO. To visualize the results, 𝐤\mathbf{k} is allowed to vary on a linear path through the Brillouin zone. The quasiparticle energy as a function of 𝐤\mathbf{k} is also called the dispersion for the system. The G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} band structure for ZnO (red lines in Figure 27) is superimposed on the experimental photoemission results shown already in Figure 2. Experiment and G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} agree very well both in terms of band positions as well as band curvatures.

Another example of a G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} band structure is shown in Figure 28 for K2Sn3O7, a new prospective ion conductor or transparent conductor [362]. The unoccupied states in the PBE band structure have been shifted up for the purposes of plotting so that the bottom of the conduction bands coincides in PBE and G0​W0​@G_{0}W_{0}@PBE. This removes the PBE band gap problem from the comparison and makes it easier to spot differences in band curvatures. For the valence bands the PBE and G0​W0​@G_{0}W_{0}@PBE band structures agree remarkably well for this material. Towards lower energies the deviations between the band structures become larger with G0​W0​@G_{0}W_{0}@PBE generally giving lower band energies than PBE. This downward shift leads to a band width widening in G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} compared to PBE. For the conduction bands, the difference between PBE and G0​W0​@G_{0}W_{0}@PBE is more pronounced. The band curvatures in G0​W0​@G_{0}W_{0}@PBE are much steeper than in PBE, which subsequently leads to a significant underestimation of the PBE bands around the X, S, U and R points in the Brillouin zone. K2Sn3O7 is another example of a material whose band gap and band structure were not known. The G0​W0​@G_{0}W_{0}@PBE band gap amounts to 3.15 eV [362], which now provides a reference value for this new material.

From the band structure, one can access the band gap, band widths, and estimate effective masses. If one models the dispersion at the band edges as parabolic, as is the case for a free particle, one can extract an effective mass from the band structure. The effective mass, labeled m∗m^{*}, is

m∗=ℏ2​[d2​Ed​k2]−1m^{*}=\hbar^{2}\left[\frac{d^{2}E}{dk^{2}}\right]^{-1} (100)

so that the band edge dispersion is

E=ℏ2​k22​m∗E=\frac{\hbar^{2}k^{2}}{2m^{*}} (101)

to mimic a free particle. In a real crystal, the effective mass is a tensor, not just a scalar. The effective mass model is closely related to the quasiparticle concept, and the renormalization factor ZsZ_{s} (Equation (39)) is one factor contributing to m∗m^{*}. The quasiparticle effective mass is usually heavier than the free electron mass because of the drag induced by the surrounding electrons. Static mean-field theories like Kohn-Sham DFT also give an estimate of effective mass from their band structure. The G​WGW band structure is typically more “curved” or concave than the Kohn-Sham structure, as shown in Figure 28, which means that G​WGW quasiparticles are “lighter” than the KS particles. In silicon and methylammonium lead iodide, the G​WGW level of theory is necessary to predict effective masses in good agreement with experiment [146, 411].

One can also compute the single-particle density of states (DOS), which in solids is analogous to taking horizontal slices through the band structure. This gives the total number of available states at the energy of that slice. In Green’s function theory, the concept of the single-particle DOS is replaced by the spectral function. The spectral function is 𝐤\mathbf{k}-dependent, so that the total effective DOS is obtained by adding up the spectral functions at all 𝐤\mathbf{k}. However, computing the spectral function requires the solution of Dyson’s equation, which is often not practical computationally. Instead, a G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} quasiparticle DOS is computed by summing up artifically broadened Gaussian peaks centered around each G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} energy. The right panel of Figure 28 shows the G0​W0​@G_{0}W_{0}@PBE DOS for K2Sn3O7 [362]. In addition, this DOS is projected on the atomic angular momentum channels ss, pp and dd. Such information is usually extracted from DFT calculations and illustrates that both the valence band and the conduction band of K2Sn3O7 is largely made up of pp states.

Band parameters like effective masses are important characteristics of semiconductors and are key parameters for the semiconductor industry. G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} effective masses are more accurate than those computed with DFT.
