These successes give G​WGW an impressive ranking in computational value, or accuracy for computational cost, on any list of first-principles electronic structure methods. The versatility of G​WGW assures that new applications in physics, chemistry, and materials science will continue to emerge in the future.

Appendix B The many-body problem

In first principles electronic structure theory, the aim is to solve the Schrödinger equation. For simplicity we focus on the non-relativistic time-independent Schrödinger equation. For a system of NN electrons and MM nuclei, the Schrödinger equation is given by

H^​Ψ=E​Ψ\hat{H}\Psi=E\Psi (117)

with the many-body Hamiltonian

H^=\displaystyle\hat{H}= −∑Ni=1∇i22+12∑Ni≠j1|ri−rj|−∑Ni=1∑Ma=1Za|ri−Ra|⏟H^e​l​e​c\displaystyle\underbrace{-\sum^{N}_{i=1}\frac{\nabla_{i}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum^{N}_{i\neq j}\frac{1}{\left|\textbf{r}_{i}-\textbf{r}_{j}\right|}-\sum^{N}_{i=1}\sum^{M}_{a=1}\frac{Z_{a}}{\left|\textbf{r}_{i}-\textbf{R}_{a}\right|}}_{\hat{H}_{elec}}
−∑Ma=1∇a22​Ma+∑Ma=1∑Mb>aZa​Zb|Ra−Rb|.\displaystyle-\sum^{M}_{a=1}\frac{\nabla_{a}^{2}}{2M_{a}}+\sum^{M}_{a=1}\sum^{M}_{b>a}\frac{Z_{a}Z_{b}}{\left|\textbf{R}_{a}-\textbf{R}_{b}\right|}. (118)

rir_{i} and RaR_{a} are the positions of the electrons and the nuclei, respectively, and ZaZ_{a} is the charge of the nuclei.

To make this system of coupled electrons and nuclei more tractable, the Born-Oppenheimer (BO) approximation of clamped nuclei is frequently introduced. In this case, we only need to consider the electronic Hamiltonian by itself,

H^e​l​e​c​Ψe​l​e​c=Ee​l​e​c​Ψe​l​e​c,\hat{H}_{elec}\Psi_{elec}=E_{elec}\Psi_{elec}, (119)

in which the many-electron wave function Ψe​l​e​c\Psi_{elec} depends parametrically on the position of the nuclei. The electronic Hamiltonian is then given by

H^e​l​e​c\displaystyle\hat{H}_{elec} =∑i=1N[−∇i22+vext​(𝐫i)]+12​∑i≠jN1|ri−rj|\displaystyle=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\left[-\frac{\nabla_{i}^{2}}{2}+v_{\rm ext}({\bf r}_{i})\right]+\frac{1}{2}\sum^{N}_{i\neq j}\frac{1}{\left|\textbf{r}_{i}-\textbf{r}_{j}\right|} (120)
=∑i=1Nh^0​(𝐫i)+12​∑i≠jNv⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j).\displaystyle=\sum^{N}_{i=1}\hat{h}^{0}({\bf r}_{i})+\frac{1}{2}\sum^{N}_{i\neq j}v({\bf r}_{i},{\bf r}_{j})\,. (121)

We use vv to denote the bare Coulomb interaction and the external potential is the same for every electron

vext(𝐫)=−∑a=1MZa|𝐫−Ra|.v_{\rm ext}({\bf r})=-\sum^{M}_{a=1}\frac{Z_{a}}{\left|{\bf r}-\textbf{R}_{a}\right|}\,. (122)

The kinetic energy and external potential are grouped together in h^0​(𝐫i)\hat{h}^{0}(\mathbf{r}_{i}) in Equation (121). Approaches to solve the electronic Schrödinger equation (119) can be largely grouped according to the basic variable they work with: the many-body wave function, the density-matrix, the density, or Green’s functions. Each choice has its advantages and disadvantages and no consensus has been reached on the optimal choice. Green’s functions have a natural connection, however, to the particle addition/removal problem and theoretical spectroscopy.

B.1 Green’s function formalism

To derive equations for the one-particle Green’s function that are more amenable to approximations than definitions in Equations (10) and (11), we start from the equation of motion for the field operators, which relates the time derivative of ψ^\hat{\psi} to the commutator of ψ^\hat{\psi} and H^e​l​e​c\hat{H}_{elec} [196, 145]:

i​∂∂t​ψ^​(𝐱,t)=[ψ^​(𝐱,t),H^e​l​e​c],i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\hat{\psi}({\bf x},t)=\left[\hat{\psi}({\bf x},t),\hat{H}_{elec}\right], (123)

where 𝐱\mathbf{x} contains also the spin variable σ\sigma, i.e., 𝐱=(𝐫,σ)\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{r},\sigma). Evaluating the commutator in the Heisenberg picture and applying the anti-commutation relations yields for the equation of motion

i​∂∂t​ψ^​(𝐱,t)=[h^0​(𝐫)+∫ψ^†​(𝐱′,t)​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)​ψ^​(𝐱′,t)​d​𝐱′]​ψ^​(𝐱,t).i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\hat{\psi}({\bf x},t)=\\ \left[\hat{h}^{0}({\bf r})+\int\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\bf x^{\prime}},t)v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})\hat{\psi}({\bf x^{\prime}},t)d{\bf x^{\prime}}\right]\hat{\psi}({\bf x},t)\,. (124)

The equation of motion for the Green’s function (10) then follows from (124)

[i​∂∂t−h^0​(𝐫)]​G​(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)=δ(t−t′)δ(𝐱−𝐱′)−i∫d𝐱′′v(𝐫,𝐫′′)×⟨N|T^​[ψ^†​(𝐱′′,t)​ψ^​(𝐱′′,t)​ψ^​(𝐱,t)​ψ^†​(𝐱′,t′)]|N⟩\left[i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}-\hat{h}^{0}({\bf r})\right]G({\bf x}t,{\bf x^{\prime}}t^{\prime})=\\ \delta(t-t^{\prime})\delta({\bf x}-{\bf x^{\prime}})-i\int\!d{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}\,v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime\prime}})\times\\ \langle N|\hat{T}\left[\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\bf x^{\prime\prime}},t)\hat{\psi}({\bf x^{\prime\prime}},t)\hat{\psi}({\bf x},t)\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\bf x^{\prime}},t^{\prime})\right]|N\rangle (125)

The term under the integral contains the two-particle Green’s function, G2​(𝐱​t,𝐱′′​t,𝐱′′​t+,𝐱′​t′)G_{2}({\bf x}t,{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t,{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t^{+},{\bf x^{\prime}}t^{\prime}), and includes all two-body correlations in the system. In order to calculate the one-particle Green’s function we would therefore require the equation of motion for the two-particle Green’s function, which in turn introduces the three-particle Green’s function. Applied iteratively, this procedure creates an infinite series of higher order Green’s functions and thus describes all the possible many-body interactions in the system. In practice, however, the resulting recurrence relation for the nthn^{\mathrm{th}} order Green’s function is impossible to solve for large nn. Instead we introduce the non-local, time-dependent self-energy Σ¯​(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)\bar{\Sigma}({\bf x}t,{\bf x^{\prime}}t^{\prime})

−i∫d𝐱′′\displaystyle-i\int\!d{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}\, v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′′)​G2​(𝐱​t,𝐱′′​t,𝐱′′​t+,𝐱′​t′)≡\displaystyle v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime\prime}})G_{2}({\bf x}t,{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t,{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t^{+},{\bf x^{\prime}}t^{\prime})\equiv
∫d​t′′​∫d​𝐱′′​Σ¯​(𝐱​t,𝐱′′​t′′)​G​(𝐱′′​t′′,𝐱′​t′).\displaystyle\int dt^{\prime\prime}\!\int\!d{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}\,\bar{\Sigma}({\bf x}t,{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t^{\prime\prime})G({\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t^{\prime\prime},{\bf x^{\prime}}t^{\prime})\,. (126)

Analogous to other electronic structure methods, we separate out the most dominant term, the Hartree potential

vH​(𝐫)\displaystyle v_{\mathrm{H}}({\bf r}) =∫d​𝐫′​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)​⟨N|​ψ^†​(𝐫′,t)​ψ^​(𝐫′,t)​|N⟩\displaystyle=\int d{\bf r^{\prime}}v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})\langle N|\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\bf r^{\prime}},t)\hat{\psi}({\bf r^{\prime}},t)|N\rangle (127)
=∫d​𝐫′​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)​n​(𝐫′),\displaystyle=\int d{\bf r^{\prime}}v({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})n({\bf r^{\prime}})\,, (128)

where n⁡(𝐫)n({\bf r}) is the electron density. With this definition, the equation of motion for the Green’s function (125) adopts the much more convenient form of an integral equation involving the self-energy, Σ=Σ¯−vH\Sigma=\bar{\Sigma}-v_{\mathrm{H}}:

[i​∂∂t−h^0​(𝐫)−vH​(𝐫)]​G​(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)=δ⁡(t−t′)​δ​(𝐫−𝐫′)+∫dt′′∫d𝐱′′Σ(𝐱t,𝐱′′t′′)G(𝐱′′t′′,𝐱′t′).\left[i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}-\hat{h}^{0}({\bf r})-v_{\mathrm{H}}({\bf r})\right]G({\bf x}t,{\bf x^{\prime}}t^{\prime})=\delta(t-t^{\prime})\delta({\bf r}-{\bf r^{\prime}})\\ +\int dt^{\prime\prime}\!\int\!d{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}\,\Sigma({\bf x}t,{\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t^{\prime\prime})G({\bf x^{\prime\prime}}t^{\prime\prime},{\bf x^{\prime}}t^{\prime})\,. (129)

If G0G_{0} now denotes the Green’s function that is a solution to h^=h^0+vH​(𝐫)\hat{h}=\hat{h}^{0}+v_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{r}) (the kinetic energy, the external potential, and the Hartree potential), then Equation (129) can be further rewritten as

G⁡(1,2)\displaystyle G(1,2) =G0​(1,2)\displaystyle=G_{0}(1,2) (130)
+∫G0(1,3)Σ(3,4)G(4,2)d(3,4).\displaystyle+\int G_{0}(1,3)\Sigma(3,4)G(4,2)d(3,4)\,.

Here we changed to the abbreviated notation (1,2,…)(1,2,\ldots) for the set of position, time and spin variables (𝐱1​t1,𝐱2​t2,…)({\bf x}_{1}t_{1},{\bf x}_{2}t_{2},\ldots). Accordingly ∫d⁡(1)\int d(1) is a shorthand notation for the integration in all three variables of the corresponding triple(s). In this context 1+1^{+} implies the addition of a positive infinitesimal to the time argument 11. Equation (130) is again Dyson’s equation [127, 128] (see also Equations (17) and (86)) and links the non-interacting Green’s function, G0G_{0}, to the interacting one, GG. Dyson’s equation gives a physical interpretation to the self-energy instead of simply its definition by Equation (126). The self-energy quantifies the difference between a bare and a fully interacting electron, or quasielectron. This brings us back to our phenomenological consideration in Section II. An additional electron or hole drags a dynamically adjusting polarization cloud through the system that alters its energy. Hence the name self-energy. If instead G0G_{0} is the solution to the mean-field Hamiltonian h^MF\hat{h}^{\mathrm{MF}} (e.g. of Kohn-Sham density-functional theory [280]) then the self-energy, Σ\Sigma, embodies the difference between a quasielectron and an electron in the static mean-field.

At this stage in the derivation, the self-energy as well as the Green’s function are still exact and contain the electron-electron interaction to all orders. A full solution of Equations (129) and (130) is not tractable and approximations are required.

B.2 Hedin’s equations

In 1965 Hedin expanded the Green’s function and the self-energy in terms of the screened instead of the bare Coulomb interaction [217]. Introducing a small perturbing field φ\varphi that will later be set to zero, the operator identity due to Schwinger [491]

G2​(1,3,2,3+)=G⁡(1,2)​G​(3,3+)−δ​G​(1,2)δ​φ​(3)G_{2}(1,3,2,3^{+})=G(1,2)G(3,3^{+})-\frac{\delta G(1,2)}{\delta\varphi(3)} (131)

can be used to eliminate the two particle Green’s function from Equation (126) for the self-energy. Multiplying the resulting equation with G−1G^{-1} leads to the following expression for the self-energy

Σ¯​(1,2)\displaystyle\bar{\Sigma}(1,2) =δ⁡(1,2)​∫d⁡(3)​v​(1,3)​G​(3,3+)\displaystyle=\delta(1,2)\int d(3)v(1,3)G(3,3^{+})
−i∫d(3,4)v(1,3)G(1,4)δ​G−1​(4,2)δ​φ​(3)\displaystyle\quad-i\int d(3,4)v(1,3)G(1,4)\frac{\delta G^{-1}(4,2)}{\delta\varphi(3)} (132)
=δ⁡(1,2)​vH​(1)\displaystyle=\delta(1,2)v_{\mathrm{H}}(1)
−i∫d(3,4)v(1,3)G(1,4)δ​G−1​(4,2)δ​φ​(3).\displaystyle\quad-i\int d(3,4)v(1,3)G(1,4)\frac{\delta G^{-1}(4,2)}{\delta\varphi(3)}\,.

where Σ¯\bar{\Sigma} is defined to include the Hartree potential vHv_{\mathrm{H}}, unlike Σ\Sigma. Using the following definitions

total potential:

V⁡(1)=φ⁡(1)+vH​(1)V(1)=\varphi(1)+v_{\mathrm{H}}(1) (133)

3-point vertex:

Γ⁡(1,2,3)=−δ​G−1​(1,2)δ​V​(3)\Gamma(1,2,3)=-\frac{\delta G^{-1}(1,2)}{\delta V(3)} (134)

dielectric function:

ε−1​(1,2)=δ​V​(1)δ​φ​(2)\varepsilon^{-1}(1,2)=\frac{\delta V(1)}{\delta\varphi(2)} (135)

screened Coulomb interaction:

W⁡(1,2)=∫d⁡(3)​ε−1​(1,3)​v​(3,2)W(1,2)=\int\!\!d(3)\;\varepsilon^{-1}(1,3)v(3,2) (136)

irreducible polarizability:

P⁡(1,2)=−i​δ​G​(1,1+)δ​V​(2)=δ​n​(1)δ​V​(2)P(1,2)=-i\frac{\delta G(1,1^{+})}{\delta V(2)}=\frac{\delta n(1)}{\delta V(2)} (137)

reducible polarizability:

χ⁡(1,2)=−i​δ​G​(1,1+)δ​φ​(2)=δ​n​(1)δ​φ​(2)\chi(1,2)=-i\frac{\delta G(1,1^{+})}{\delta\varphi(2)}=\frac{\delta n(1)}{\delta\varphi(2)} (138)

we arrive at Hedin’s equations [217]

P⁡(1,2)\displaystyle P(1,2) =−i∫d(3,4)G(4,2)G(2,3)Γ(3,4,1)\displaystyle=-i\!\!\int\!\!d(3,4)G(4,2)G(2,3)\Gamma(3,4,1) (139)
W⁡(1,2)\displaystyle W(1,2) =v⁡(1,2)+∫d⁡(3,4)​v​(1,3)​P​(3,4)​W​(4,2)\displaystyle=v(1,2)+\!\!\int\!\!d(3,4)v(1,3)P(3,4)W(4,2) (140)
Σ⁡(1,2)\displaystyle\Sigma(1,2) =i​∫d⁡(3,4)​G​(1,4)​W​(1+,3)​Γ​(4,2,3)\displaystyle=i\int\!\!d(3,4)G(1,4)W(1^{+},3)\Gamma(4,2,3) (141)
Γ⁡(1,2,3)\displaystyle\Gamma(1,2,3) =δ⁡(1,2)​δ​(1,3)+\displaystyle=\delta(1,2)\delta(1,3)+ (142)
∫d⁡(4,5,6,7)​δ​Σ​(1,2)δ​G​(4,5)​G​(4,6)​G​(7,5)​Γ​(6,7,3).\displaystyle\hskip-11.38092pt\!\!\int\!\!d(4,5,6,7)\frac{\delta\Sigma(1,2)}{\delta G(4,5)}G(4,6)G(7,5)\Gamma(6,7,3).

Dyson’s equation (130) closes this set of integro-differential equations, which is shown pictorially in Figure 24(a).

The benefit of Hedin’s equations is that the self-energy is given in terms of an effective, or screened, rather than the bare Coulomb interaction

W⁡(1,2)=∫d⁡(3)​ε−1​(1,3)​v​(3,2).W(1,2)=\int\!\!d(3)\>\varepsilon^{-1}(1,3)v(3,2)\>. (143)

The screening

ε−1​(1,2)=δ⁡(1,2)+∫d⁡(3)​v​(1,3)​χ​(3,2)\varepsilon^{-1}(1,2)=\delta(1,2)+\int\!\!d(3)\>v(1,3)\chi(3,2) (144)

follows from the reducible polarizability or density-density response function

χ⁡(1,2)\displaystyle\chi(1,2) =χ0​(1,2)+∫d⁡(3,4)​χ0​(1,3)​v​(3,4)​χ​(4,2)\displaystyle=\chi_{0}(1,2)+\int\!\!d(3,4)\chi_{0}(1,3)v(3,4)\chi(4,2)
=⟨N|T^​[δ​n^​(1)​δ​n^​(2)]|N⟩.\displaystyle=\langle N|\hat{T}\left[\delta\hat{n}(1)\delta\hat{n}(2)\right]|N\rangle\>. (145)

Here δ​n^​(1)\delta\hat{n}(1) is a density fluctuation δ​n^​(1)=n^​(1)−n​(1)\delta\hat{n}(1)=\hat{n}(1)-n(1) of the density around its average value, where n^​(1)=∑iNδ⁡(r1−ri)\hat{n}(1)=\sum_{i}^{N}\delta(r_{1}-r_{i}). For a polarizable medium, like a solid, screening is large and the screened Coulomb interaction will differ considerably from the bare one. It therefore makes sense to build a perturbation series on WW instead of vv. Hedin’s equations are physically transparent in this sense. Electron-hole pairs are created in the polarizability (one Green’s function for the electron, a separate Green’s function for the hole). They interact through the vertex function, which is determined by the change in potential upon excitation. The polarizability, in turn, determines the dielectric function, which screens the Coulomb interaction. The self-energy quantifies the energy contribution that the added electron or hole experiences through the interaction with its surrounding.

Appendix C Computational details

Figures 11, 12, 14, 16(b), 18, 25 and 35 present original content. All calculations are performed with the FHI-aims program package [61, 216], which expands the all-electron KS equations in numeric-atom-centered orbitals (NAOs), see Section IV.4. The structures have been optimized at the DFT level using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional [402] to model the XC potential and NAOs of tier 2 quality [61] to represent core and valence electrons. Dispersion corrections are accounted for by employing the Tkatchenko-Scheffler van der Waals correction [555].

G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} calculations have been performed with the contour-deformation (CD) technique [189] if not indicated otherwise. Calculations with the analytic continuation (AC) [437] have been conducted for the G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} self-energies in Figure 14 and for the scG​WGW result in Figure 18. For both methods, CD and AC, a modified Gauss-Legendre grid with 200 grid points is used for the numerical integration of the integral over the imaginary frequency axis. In case of the AC approach, the same set of grid points {i​ω}\{i\omega\} is employed to calculate Σsc​(i​ω)\Sigma^{c}_{s}(i\omega), which has been fitted to a Padé approximant with at least 16 parameters [569], unless stated otherwise.

Quasiparticle energies have been computed by iteratively solving Equation (26). Furthermore, all quasiparticle energies have been extrapolated to the complete basis set limit using the Dunning basis set family cc-pVnnZ (n=3−6)(n=3-6) [122, 589]. The cc-pVnnZ basis sets are all-electron Gaussian basis sets, which can be considered as a special case of an NAO and are treated numerically in FHI-aims. The extrapolation has been performed by a linear regression against the inverse of the total number of basis functions.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
